utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you understand that you are still under the oath that you took on Friday to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, at the end of the proceedings on Friday you were telling us about events at the beginning of April of 1992. You had told us about your wife leaving Kozarac on that day. I would like you to tell us now where she went on that day of 1st April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family left for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say your "family", was that your children as well as your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife, my daughter Valentina, my daughter Aleksandra and my mother Staka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When they went to Banja Luka did you travel with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you travel to Banja Luka on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We travelled in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whose van was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my brother's van, my brother Ljubomir. It was a white van, Volkswagen van.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your family stay in Banja Luka on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went back and they stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From Banja Luka did they travel elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went to the village of Kozice in the vicinity of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for going to Kozice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the main reason was a general feeling of unsafety in the territory of Kozarac which lasted for a longer period of time. So, simply, I saw that many people were leaving Kozarac and me and my wife were concerned about our children. I was living in Kozarac alone with my old mother (who was quite sick at that time) and my three year old daughter and another daughter and my wife. So the place I was at that moment was at the centre of Kozarac. It was quite an awkward position in view of the circumstances in Kozarac at that time. At that time there was some kind of mobilization going on in Kozarac. People were being called up, and most of the families knew where they would go to find shelter in case of war. Those who had a place to go, they left, they mostly left. People who had relatives abroad, either in Germany or Slovenia or elsewhere, people were leaving in coaches, by cars, and by planes. There used to be a regular service Banja Luka/Belgrade by plane at that time. So, I did not manage to find out whether I should go to seek for a shelter in case of war and I could see that there were intensive preparations going on for the protection of the population, but nobody informed me about that. So, I felt somehow isolated and, in view of those circumstances, I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the connection with Kozice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother Mladen was the best man of Majkic, the priest, and because of that relation, that connection, he used to visit our house from time to time and we visited each other. Why Kozice? I think my wife could give you an answer because she had made an agreement with Majkic's wife. They were on very good terms, the two of them, and I think that was the only reason. Maybe also because several days before our departure there had been an incident in Kozarac. I do not know what holiday it was, but at one moment the priest's wife came to my house. She was holding a several months old baby in her arms and she was crying. I did not understand what was going on and I just know that my mother went to see her and they went to their home. When I came back to see what had happened, she told me that that day unknown persons had tried to remove the flag from the church, and that she was threatened that she would be killed and that she had to take off that flag. So she did not know what to do, her husband was not at home at that time. I know that she informed the police about that, and I know that police from Kozarac arrived and the situation somehow calmed down. Anyhow, similar incidents were all too frequent for men to feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In evidence in this Court we heard the allegation that was reported as a result of other people telling others that you had attempted to set fire to the Serb Orthodox church in Kozarac. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I never tried to do such a thing and it never occurred to me to do something like that, and I think that no one ever tried to set the church, the Orthodox church, on fire -- no one. There used to be a similar story and I was surprised to learn -- actually I learnt it here for the first time -- the story about this attempt to burn down the church, but there was a similar story in connection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Kozice with your family or did you return to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go with them right away. I know that I visited them in the village of Kozice once. My wife and my family were staying with the parents of Veselka Majkic, the priest's wife, not with his parents but with her parents. I know that her mother lived there with a younger sister and I know that Veselka's father was living in Austria at the time. So I visited them, I do not know exactly when, but I visited them once and I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst your family were away during this time, did you continue to run the cafe bar in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The cafe was open all the time throughout that period, some six months before the beginning of war operations in the Prijedor territory. I had one waiter working for me. I think that his name was Elvir or Elvis Softic. It was a young man and he worked for me very long and the last six months he worked alone. I trusted him. He had a key of my cafe, so if I was absent he would open the cafe himself. He ran it all by himself. There were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your family returned from Kozice and rejoined you in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 29th April, they came back. I was surprised. I was not expecting them, but they thought that danger had been gone, that the situation has improved in Kozarac. However, quite opposite actually happened. On that day when I arrived there was a general chaos in Kozarac. I do not remember seeing civilians in the street. Everybody was armed, and it was really a chaos. It was not easy to recognise which soldiers belonged to which army. You could see all kinds of insignia. You simply could not tell who was with whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did they stay in Kozarac for on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed in Kozarac until 3rd May. I say 3rd May because on that day another incident occurred, an incident which was just too much for everybody in Kozarac. I remember that on that day my wife, I think it was Sunday or weekend, I do not know exactly which day, and she was with her parents in Vidovici on that day, and I was at home with my mother. All of a sudden I heard people screaming, and I got out to find out what was happening and neighbours panicked. Everybody was all of a sudden in shelters and I asked what was going on, and then they said that a tank had arrived near Kozarac and there was a danger of imminent war. So I went to the lower part of Kozarac down the street of Marsala Tita and near the triangle which has been shown here quite often. I saw on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road a tank which was pointing to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you on that particular day leave Kozarac with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but before that several incidents had happened which made me leave Kozarac. When I saw the tank, when I talked to some people and I realised everybody was armed, there was a group of armed people standing next to Bosko Dragicevic's house and there was general chaos. I went to see the priest, Majkic. I asked him what was going on because he was closer to the event, and he did not know anything about what was going on. I asked some other people and they told me that a kind of incident had occurred and then we tried to do something. People asked us to do something. They told us, "Well, you are Serbs. You should do something". I said, "OK, we will try to do something". So we went, he and I went, along a road near the church and we got to the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road, and we set off in the direction where the tank was and we were moving from the direction of Banja Luka towards Prijedor, but after 100 or 150 metres from the right side of the road some unknown persons ordered us to go back. They said, "You should go back otherwise we will shoot". We were afraid so we went back. Later on, I was thinking I really do not know why we went because it was quite dangerous and at that moment I did not fully realise the extent of the danger. So we went back to his house and he suggested that we should leave; that would be the best thing. So I left. I went back to my house and my wife had come back from the village of Vidovici in the meantime together with my children. We packed very quickly. We went back to Majkic and we all got into his car. There was a lot of panic going on. I remember I did not take anything with me, no clothes. We were eight in his car. It was a Jugo 45 type of car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you own a car at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have a car. I used to own a car in the period when I was working in Banja Luka for about three years. I had a Visa Citroen. I sold it when I left for Libya and after that I never owned a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The priest's car that you referred to, that zastava, did you all fit in this car, the eight of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because we did not have any belongings with us, we just got in very quickly. It was a big haste and the priest was driving and I was sitting at the front passenger seat and behind there was my mother, my wife, my daughter Valentina, Aleksandra, and the wife of the priest was also sitting there, Veselka and her daughter who was several months old. We were all very cramped. I was at the front so I did not really feel that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which route did the car take out of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since we realised, we knew, that the tank was at the entrance to the town of Kozarac, we thought that it was impossible to take that road. So we took the old Banja Luka road in the direction of Banja Luka, and we thought that we could get to the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and continue our journey towards Banja Luka because the old road is parallel to the new one, and there are several spots where you merge. So we went along that road and after 100 metres we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The old road you referred to, does that run past the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you took that road in the direction of Banja Luka, it at some stage comes close to what is called the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most of it runs parallel with that road, very close, maybe some 100 metres at some spots or maybe 50, but on many spots when you drive towards Banja Luka, the two roads merge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you try to get on to the new highway towards Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the idea. After maybe 500 metres driving in the direction of Banja Luka along the old road, you could pull into the main, into the new Prijedor/Banja Luka road. I do not recall exactly the name of that spot, but that is what people mostly did when they travelled to Banja Luka because it is closer for about one kilometre as opposed to when you go to the junction, Prijedor/Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you able to get out of Kozarac and travel to Banja Luka on that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was surprised because after 100 metres we were stopped, as I told you. The priest talked to the man who was standing in the middle of the road, that side road. I knew that young man who was standing there. He was holding a rifle and he had a uniform, a military uniform. It was Bahonjic and I think his name is Sead, I am not quite sure, but I knew him very well because he had a private business for production of coffee machines. So I knew him very well and he sold me the coffee machine for my cafe. He was standing there. He pointed his rifle and he said that he was under orders not to let us leave Kozarac. So I asked him once again. He first talked to the priest. He was standing some 20 metres away. So I opened the door and I asked him, I begged him, to let us leave, and I said, "I will just drive my wife and children. I will come back. If you want me to stay here, I will come back. There is no problem". He said, "No, we are under orders no one should leave Kozarac". "Who ordered that?" He said, "I do not know". He did not want to answer my question. So at that moment I realised that on the left side there was a large group of people standing behind a shelter and I said, "Well, OK. I will go to the police to ask for the permission to leave Kozarac", and he said, "Well, please do so". We went along the road. I do not know the exact name of that street, maybe Omladinska or Pionirska. Anyway, it is the street that leads to the hospital in Kozarac, the health centre. At the health centre it turns left and goes to the main street, Marsala Tita, which leads to Mrakovica. So we went along that road, in the direction of the police station, which is in the main street, Marsala Tita Street, but we did not stop there because there was a huge group of people standing in front of the police station and everybody was armed. We simply could not stop. So I saw that many people were carrying weapons and there were vehicles were passing by and you could no longer tell there was any kind of order at that time. People were driving both on the left and the right side of the road. It was a general chaos. So we drove on in the direction of Mrakovica and I remember that they tried to stop us near the village of Rajkovici. I know there was a well at that spot which was some kind of monument, so a soldier wearing the same uniform as the previous one tried to stop us. But this one had a semi-automatic rifle and he also had a hand held rocket launcher fixed to his rifle. I knew that man too. It was Salkanovic. They called him "Salkan", but I do not know his real name. So he tried to stop us, but we just drove past very fast and went on in the direction of Mrakovica. So, we were travelling towards Mrakovica, via the village of Podgradje. We arrived in Gradiska and then from Gradiska we set on in the direction of Banja Luka where we arrived in the evening. I know that we drove some 150 kilometres that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to help those listening to the evidence in this case, if I can just identify a number of those streets that you referred to? You referred to leaving the old road and going up towards the health centre in Kozarac. Is that a road that is at right angles to the old road and virtually opposite the church itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That road goes past the house of Marinko Konjivoda on the right side, Mirko Grahovac's house on the left side, Bestalic Meho's house, and it leads right to the entrance of the health centre in Kozarac and at triangles it turns left and merges with the main street, Marsala Tita Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not have a photograph of that street immediately to hand, but you may remember when a witness was giving evidence, an anonymous witness, that he looked at a photograph of that street but was unable to identify it. Was that the street you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The direction that you took out of Kozarac towards Mrakovica and that would have been up Marsala Tita Street and the continuation of Marsala Tita Street out of Kozarac, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Marsala Tita Street goes on and it passes the villages of Dera, Rajkovici. It goes past the youth settlement, Benkovac, and it leads to Mrakovica which is the top of the Kozara mountain. From Mrakovica, you turn left from where you can only take a macadam road and after a couple of kilometres there is an asphalt road. So the road leading from Gradiska to Banja Luka, that is the road Banja Luka/Bosanska Gradiska which we used to take when travelling to Belgrade. It is a main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Banja Luka, where did you go to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to my brother's place, Ljubomir's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that he has an apartment in a block of flats in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not really an apartment. It was some sort of provisional accommodation. It was not a real apartment. It was in basement and there was also -- there was only one room in that basement which served both as the kitchen and bedroom. There was also a bedroom, a sort of makeshift bathroom improvised by my brother. I know that he moved there after the earthquake in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I had asked you about was where your brother Ljubo lived in Banja Luka, what sort of accommodation he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly what I just described, that is where he lived, and the settlement is called Starcevica. Those were really -- it was a basement unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you stay with your brother Ljubo or did you go to live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all spent the night there. It was very late when we arrived and the priest did not have a place to go. We suggested that he stayed. It was risky. We did not know what was going to go on. We did not know what was happening on the other roads, how you could get to Sanski Most. You could get there through Mrkonic Grad. He himself did not know at the time where he was going to go, to his parents or somewhere else. So, simply, we did not know what was going on. He stayed the night and the next day he left. I later found out that he went back to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you continue to stay with your brother Ljubo or did you go to live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent several days at my brother's and throughout that time my wife and myself cleaned up another residential unit in Koste Jarica Street which was not in a very good condition. We tried to make it livable where we could move in for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at some photographs, Exhibit 62A and B, please? Defence 62A and B. If those photographs actually could be put straightaway on the monitor? We see on the left-hand side a photograph of a house with a gate in front of it. Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a house in Koste Jarica Street in Starcevica settlement in Banja Luka where I moved my family in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you come to stay in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself and my family and my brother had a friend, Nihad Alic -- he was a salesman like my brother -- and in the course of time we all met. He was in very -- he had a very good relationship with my brother Ljubomir and he used to come to Kozarac in earlier times quite a lot, especially -- he had offered to my brother for us to move into that house. The previous residents, that is, the owners, the woman had left, she went abroad, and her husband had died or was killed, I do not remember exactly, so Nedim had the key and they offered us to move there. The house had -- it was about 50 metres, maybe less, down the road. We met and he showed us this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which part of the house did you move into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved into the basement which can be seen on the right-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To get to the basement where would you find it in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you look at the left-hand side photograph you can see an improvised gate there. You would turn right and go around. You would come to the entrance from the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is the house itself standing on a slope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The front side, if you look at the left-hand side photograph, that is -- this is all flat, the yard and the path, but in the back of the house the ground slopes down on a decline, and about 50 metres down there is a little creek and it is sort of grown in, overgrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph D62B, which is the one on the right-hand side, what does that show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shows the basement which you can see on the left-hand side photograph, but it is part of the same structure, of the same building. In that period, while I was staying with my brother, I tried to clean up, make it livable. My friend, Hamdija, who was a professional in there, we first painted the kitchen and that living area, so-called, even though only the kitchen really existed, it was ready to be lived in, and the rest of the structure was pretty useless. So we tried to make it usable. So I was interested in putting there my wife and my mother. But, under normal circumstances, in normal conditions, nobody would live there. The windows were broken on the side. People had broken into the building several times while the owner was abroad. That was one of the reasons why Nedim offered us to move there because the very presence would deter people, and there were several break-ins that were happening in that area. So it was beneficial for them too. To the left from the entrance there was a large room which was about half of the square area of the house. There was a sofa and armoire, but everything was dirty and we kept cleaning it and it had a bad stench. So I moved the family in, but every time I would come we kept cleaning and cleaning out. I remembered behind that living room area there was a room where they had a large cooler. I -- we found a freezer. We found a lot of spoiled food in there. So it gave a terrible stench. I know that throughout the time we stayed there we kept cleaning it out and we never finished. There was no bathroom there. I heard my wife say that the conditions were good, but it is not right. Maybe they were better than what they had in the village of Kozice, maybe. I know that there was no bathroom in this house and the toilet was improvised. When we wanted to take a bath we would go to my brother's or to our friend's, to the family (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your family move into this accommodation with you or did you live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I was staying in Banja Luka all up until we moved them in and then I went back to the Kozarac. On the right-hand side photograph on that tree you can see an iron bar, and that was a TV antennae that I put up right away so that my family could maybe watch television. At that time we had no TV, but we found the antennae so I just installed it. Later, my brother brought a TV so we could watch it. But, in general, they were bad conditions. We were embarrassed to invite anybody so that they could see where we lived. I had a lot of friends in Banja Luka but I did not invite them. They all knew that I lived very well in Kozarac, and for me it was embarrassing to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said you arrived in Banja Luka on 3rd May. About what would the date have been that your family moved into that accommodation in Koste Jarica street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 6th May, several days, three or four, maybe it was 7th May, but I think it was 6th. I also know well that there is also a well there to the right because nothing inside really worked. It seems to me that people -- they must have been taking baths outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When they moved in on 6th or 7th May, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day I went back to Kozarac, because my cafe was still open, and the young man that I told you about, Elvir, my waiter, he knew that I was not coming. He had a key. He would open up and he knew his job. He was keeping the books, and so I just joined him and we continued. Also, we had a special relationship. He was not asking many questions where I was going, when I was coming back, and I was not very strict towards him. So we got along very well. So my presence or absence did not interfere with the work. He knew his job, even if there was -- if we ran out of beverage, he would go to Adil Jakupovic, Sefik Arnautovic, and he would take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had returned to Kozarac; did there come a time when you eventually left Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I left Kozarac 23rd May '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you some questions about that period until 23rd May 1992. Did you visit your family in Banja Luka on occasions during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I said, I trusted this young man and it was no problem for me to leave. He had the keys both to the cafe and to my house and to the garage where there were supplies of alcoholic and other beverages. I often went mostly because I always took something with me. Once we -- when we first left Kozarac, we almost took nothing with us, very few things, especially when the children's things, they had no clothes. There was nothing in Banja Luka. I also remember that I took bedding. All there was in that house, everything was really neglected, and we only had one blanket so you had to fold it underneath and over your head so that you could fall asleep. There were no conditions there. So I very often went there and took things with me. It was difficult because I did not have a vehicle. We had to find a way, a bus or a truck, or find somebody who was going. So that is how I was going there. But, mostly I would not stay there; I would go and then I would come back the same day or the next. I was not staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your brother Ljubomir described taking a TV set and a terrier dog back to Banja Luka on your behalf. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is right, but it was not one terrier. It was two of them. They are small dogs. Maybe they were three weeks or a month old. One he took and one we left with the family where we stayed in Banja Luka, but I had a large terrier which was their mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I think we need to know about it for the moment. It was just the fact of it rather than the dog family history. During this period until 23rd May, we know from evidence that on 29th April 1992 there was the takeover in Prijedor and the Crisis Staff was formed in Prijedor. I want to ask you now about this period of time from 29th April until 23rd May. Is it right that there were a series of meetings that took place between the new authorities in Prijedor and representatives from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those meetings concerned a series of ultimata that had been given to Kozarac. Were you aware of these ultimata?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew, but all that started by takeover of the power. I first found out and it was a shock to me. To a degree, one could understand the takeover of power, but I was shocked when I saw that the next day some people were turned back. They could not go to work. Some said that they were turned back at Orlovci and some said, "We could not go there; there are flags hanging around town". That is the first shock. That is what shocked the population, the general population, who was not familiar with this. But then I think that the whole thing went on for much longer, even before the takeover, and that the official authorities in Kozarac knew about it but not the general population. But, after the takeover on 29th April until 23rd May, there were several additional meetings and there were these ultimata that were coming from the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. I heard about them and I know about the ultimatums that were given to the police force in Kozarac, to the regular police. They were not directed to the civilians and the TO and the reserve police. I heard only about the ultimatums sent by the police in Prijedor to the active police force in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that there were a number of delegations from the municipality of Kozarac, and citizens who were part of the municipality met those within the Crisis Staff in Prijedor to discuss the state of affairs with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not that familiar about this first period, after the takeover. Later, when I joined the civic forum, I found out, talking to people, that these negotiations went on for a long time, and there were representatives of Local Commune of Kozarac taking part and the representatives of the police force, and they were talking to the people from the municipalities. But, Kemal Susic told me that these negotiations were interrupted at one point, maybe about two weeks before the hostilities began. He told me that they had formed a citizens' forum which would be non-partisan. There may have been some party members in it but, by and large, they organised and they wanted to join the negotiations precisely because the negotiations between the local authorities in Kozarac and in Prijedor had been interrupted. So, Kemal Susic and other citizens who before that had no active part in the Local Commune, they visited me and they asked me if I would join the same forum. I asked them about the reasons for it and they told me what was going on before. That is why they wanted to come and try to help in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that the citizens forum approached you to join them and take a part in their discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was a simple one. They said, Kemal Susic explained, I had contact and we talked and, first of all, they knew who my father was, that he was a well-known person in the municipality and they thought that I could help as his son. Also they said that they would also invite Bosko Dragicevic. His son was the first President of the Kozara municipality earlier, and so they were talking about the possibility of creating a mutual trust. They said that they would also invite several other people who were non-Muslims in Kozarac. I agreed with that but, frankly speaking, at first I was not sure. I did not know about the real goals of this forum. I was afraid that all people would be manipulated by any which party. It was risky to get involved because you did not know what was behind it. We did not know what was going on at the very top. We did not know about the previous negotiations. We just knew that there were ultimatums, that there was something going on in that respect. So we went to Prijedor with quite a bit of -- with many unknowns. We knew one thing. We wanted to quiet down the situation, to improve relationships with Prijedor and Banja Luka and we thought of no other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can tell the translators are working at great speed to keep up with you, Mr. Tadic. If you could speak a little bit slower because they are trying to interpret every word. I can tell they are moving very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what was the date that Mr. Tadic joined the citizens' forum or civic forum?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will ask that question. Thank you, your Honour. [To the witness]: Can you tell us when it was you decided to join the civic forum as a result of Kemal Susic approaching you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 10th May. In the period between 10th and 23rd May we met twice in Prijedor. I remember that the last time when we met, it was 20th May. The first meeting I do not recall exactly, but it was during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the first meeting that you would have attended that you cannot recall the date, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot say if it was 11th or 12th, but it was that first meeting, and then we -- after we had an agreement, we did certain things and then another meeting followed which was on 20th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In both of these meetings that took place, did you play any active role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I took Kemal Susic's invitation very seriously. Then when I saw who the other members were, I really started believing the good intentions. Those were people who were not involved in the war. They were interested in business or sports, the communal living, so these were the people with whom we lived. They were my neighbours or my brothers, the people from the centre of Kozarac, who were considered to be the natives. There was Jusuf Pasic, the doctor, Kemal Balic, Hamdija Kahrimanovic, Dragoje Pupovac from Kozarusa. Bosko Dragicevic was present at the first meeting, but then refused. Ilijaz Memic was also representing the Local Commune and then he also refused to come to the second meeting and he fled abroad with his family. He was a representative of the SDA and the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the first meeting what was discussed between the various bodies who were present and represented? What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that first it should be explained how the meeting came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could actually answer my question first about the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subject was the ultimatum that was given to the police and security situation in the area of Kozarac, the Local Commune. The Local Commune of Kozarac was part of the Prijedor municipality. The main institutions were in the city of Prijedor however you felt about it, and there was a municipal Crisis Staff that was instituted there and they had the superior authority. They took over all power. At that time the civilian government did not function the way it used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The representations made by the people from the civic forum in Kozarac, were they representations and were they presented in a way that you supported and agreed with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had arrived there because we wanted to hear about what the problem was because we did not really know what the problem was, and they told us what the problem was. It was exposed by a person whom I met there for the first time, by Simo Drljaca, a new chief of the Prijedor police. He mainly had the floor although the meeting was also attended by the Commander of the municipal Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic and Mico Kovacevic, who was the President of the Executive Council, was also there, the President of the SDS, Simo Miskovic. There were several people in military uniforms which I had never seen before. But mainly the problems were the relations between Kozarac police and Prijedor police, and that is why Simo Drljaca had the floor most of the time. He explained everything in very strict terms, and he said what the problems were and they did not want to talk about that, and they said who we were representing and so on. "How will you implement what we agree?" and so on. The only power at that time in Kozarac, it was in Memic's, Ilijaz Memic's hands. So they did not know whether everything we can agree would be implemented. So I know that Simo Drljaca explained, exposed, his requests. He asked that active policemen sign loyalty to the new government in Prijedor, to the police chief, that insignia be changed and uniforms, or otherwise people who are fully employed there with the police, then they should leave the police and give back the weapons. Those were his main requests, requests of the Chief of Police in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca. He explained his requests and he also issued some kind of ultimatum. He said that it was the order of the Banja Luka centre of public safety, headed by Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The delegation that you were asked to join from the civic forum in Kozarac, did you have an agreed policy amongst yourselves? Did you actually have any power amongst yourselves to respond or to in some way comply with this ultimatum from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that precisely was the big problem. We didn’t have any authority, not that I knew of. Maybe some people did have some kind of instructions but they did not say anything about them. There was a very serious problem because in case we should come to an agreement, how could we possibly implement it? So the only person who had some authority in Kozarac at that time was Ilijaz Memic, also Bosko Dragicevic. Bosko Dragicevic was a member of the Executive Council of the Local Commune and Ilijaz Memic was a representative of the SDA. They refused to co-operate. Bosko Dragicevic justified himself by being very busy and Memic simply packed his things and fled abroad, so we just -- we remained stranded. Anyhow, there was a possibility to do something. That is why members of the forum suggested a meeting of the Assembly of the citizens of Kozarac which was held, and they explained to them the requests issued by the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor. I did not attend that Assembly, but we agreed that we should go to Prijedor once again. I think it was on 20th May that we went back to Prijedor and had another meeting. The same people attended the meeting, municipal Crisis Staff from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The meeting in the Assembly in Kozarac, the people's Assembly, can you recollect when that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was held after our first meeting in Prijedor. It was the usual procedure, because after the meeting we managed somehow to find an agreement. We agreed that the ultimatum should be postponed because the Chief of Police in Prijedor, Drljaca, he had said what the exact date should be to implement the ultimatum. So we managed to postpone it until the next meeting which took place on 20th. Our representatives told that to the citizens in Kozarac, to the Assembly, and a new meeting took place then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just ask you about the Citizens Assembly in Kozarac? You said that you did not attend that meeting. Can you recollect what the reason was, why you were not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be frank, I simply could not. I was not allowed. I trusted people whom I went with but they were also afraid. Many of them were being threatened by some individuals. They were treated as some sort of traitors in case anything should be agreed. So I simply could not go to that meeting. But Kemal Susic informed me about the meeting and the results. He came to see me after that, and he told me nothing special happened, people dominated there, the same people who had attended other meetings in Prijedor, and they simply stuck to their proposals. Some new people appeared, people who had not lived in Kozarac before that. There was a major who came to the meeting. I think that his name was Menkovic, Mirsad Menkovic, and Kemal told me it was unbelievable what was going on at the Assembly. Some groups insisted that the weapons should not be given back and that the loyalty should not be signed. There were people who were looking for a compromise. Anyhow, the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this stage, it was obviously well-known that it had been a Serb takeover of power in Prijedor, and you referred to your difficulties in being able to attend that meeting. Was that because lines were being drawn now between Serbs and the Muslims far clearer than they had been in the previous time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the takeover in the municipality of Prijedor did create a certain animosity towards us who were living in the centre of Kozarac, a certain mistrust, because it all took place quite unexpectedly in Prijedor. It was a shock for everybody, because the local government was in the hands of the SDA, a Muslim party in Prijedor, and something like a coup had happened. Of course, people no longer believed anyone. They would simply turn their heads away because it was difficult to believe, to trust, someone, they identified the power with someone who had done something terrible. They sided us somehow with them, identified us with them. So what I was trying to do, I was just trying to help, as far as it was possible for me, because I was from the centre of Kozarac because my parents had been living there and I thought that I could do something, and it was my duty to do something. But, as I say, there were many groups of people who were spreading lies. I don’t know if it was all on purpose, but simple people were disappointed. Power had been taken away and, on the other hand, everybody was acquiring weapons in Kozarac. The weapons were being openly sold and you no longer knew whom to trust. There was a general feeling of insecurity, and those who were not organised in some units, paramilitary units, or police units, they simply turned away to their own families and they just cared about that. They wanted to shelter their families and that was the life, that was the situation in Kozarac until May '92. There was very little communication between people at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The second meeting that took place in Prijedor, can you tell us what was discussed at that meeting and what the atmosphere was like on the 20th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that meeting did bring some hope that things would be solved at the level of the Kozarac Local Commune, because Drljaca said, although he had already said that ultimata that had been issued came from Banja Luka, from the centre of security services, but he denounced that because he said at the second meeting, "OK, well, you do not have to change insignia but you have to sign loyalty". So there was some kind of progress and we said, "Well, OK, when it comes to insignia, then the police in Kozarac don’t have to wear hats either". So you had a possibility of putting the insignia on other parts of the uniform. But, anyhow, we managed to obtain for those insignia not to be changed. But there was a compromise because hats were no longer worn. That was some kind of progress. But the municipal staff, there was always someone -- there was a representative of the military who mentioned the problem of paramilitary units in Kozarac, because in the area of Kozarac there had been several incidents, mostly on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road. People would stop columns of soldiers that were coming back from the front in Croatia, and sometimes a Serbian reserve soldier would be arrested by a group of, I do not know, Suljo Kosuran or someone else, and they would be detained. So it was very unsafe to walk around Kozarac for everyone, everybody who belonged to either the JNA or the Krajina army. So, as I say, some steps had been made, but the problem was the signing of loyalty. Drljaca did say that if the chief of the Banja Luka police allows, then loyalty would not have to be signed. So those were the discussions that we had, and we wanted to go to Banja Luka around 20th, 21st May, in order to reach any kind of agreement. So, aside from that ultimatum, there was an agreement also that people who were not allowed to carry weapons and who were walking around with weapons had to store their weapons at home. So there was a kind of agreement but, as I say, our group was not allowed to do anything. We could just listen to the proposal and propose something, but we were not in charge. We could not say, "OK, it is going to be implemented" because there was a very strict group of people in Kozarac, people with criminal records, such as Suljo Kusuran who had a group of people under weapons. That was this Cirkin person, I do not know his name, but he was in Kozarusa, who also had a criminal record. They just organised some groups themselves and they were doing everything they pleased. So that created an image of Kozarac. Well, whether the official authorities of Kozarac could prevent such kind of organising of people, that was a question. I remember that they were saying that some 20 policemen were ready to sign loyalty, but when those paramilitary groups heard about that, they said, "If you sign loyalty, you would be liquidated, you and your families". So that was some sort of capitulation at that time. There were always some individuals who exacerbated the situation and which we had all found ourselves. There was a group of people in Prijedor a group headed by Duca Knezevic. There was a group in Omarska. They communicated among themselves. It was some sort of competition which went to the expense of the man in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period from 20th May, the second meeting that took place in Prijedor, and 24th May, the day of the attack on Kozarac, was there any opportunity for the representatives from the civic forum to report back to the Citizens Assembly in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the civic -- the last Citizens Assembly in Kozarac was held on 21st May '92. We had previously agreed in Prijedor that the Assembly would be attended by a representative from the Crisis Staff, and we were told that Simo Miskovic would attend the Assembly together with Dragan Savanovic, who was at that time Vice President of the municipality and Deputy Commander of the municipal Crisis Staff. They attended the Assembly and I was not present at the meeting. I did not want to be with them because I thought that people would identify me with them, and I think that they were not honest in front of those people. Although Simo Miskovic was trusted by the people in Kozarac because his father used to work as a policeman in Kozarac, he lived there for a very long period of his life and he knew many people in Kozarac. I know he knew Sefik Arnautovic, who was a prominent, respectable citizen in Kozarac. So people trusted him. People believed that he would do something, but I think that he himself was not in the position to do anything special, because he had the Commander of the municipal Crisis Staff behind him and all the military leadership. I know that that meeting was held, but, later on people described to me what had been happening there. There were some disagreements and there was a verbal conflict. I do not know what was being suggested by the representative of the Crisis Staff, but at that time all relations with the Crisis Staff in Prijedor were severed. I remember that, and my neighbours told me, that the same Major Mirsad appeared and he said, "I would rather kill myself than be forced to sign any kind of loyalty to Prijedor. That would be a total capitulation". So they created an unhealthy atmosphere. So they voted that the weapons would not be given back, that the loyalty would not be signed, and the police of Kozarac had previously indicated that if the citizens of Kozarac should decide so, they would sign loyalty. But, as I say, under the pressure of those extremists, that did not happen. So all we could do was try to organise a meeting in Banja Luka. We did have a meeting. I talked with Susic again and with Balic and we had the intention of going to Banja Luka, but it was all too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The ultimatum that was eventually delivered to Kozarac was the, an ultimatum with a deadline of noon on 24th May 1992. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I do not know whether there was exact time very strict ultimatum. Maybe it had been issued, but I do not know. The meetings which we attended were also attended by the representatives of the military in Prijedor and the police. But there was a general chaos at that time. I did not know who the persons in charge were, who members of the Crisis Staff were. Anyway, we were not aware of that ultimatum. That is why we thought, that’s why we wanted to go to Banja Luka, to try and ask for mercy from the President of the security services centre. So there was an attempt. There was an ultimatum, but it was not the last one because the municipal Crisis Staff would always come up with some new conditions. So I don’t think that we would have achieved anything, and the conflict -- the new problems were being created every day. I remember there was a very serious incident in Kozarac on 22nd May. My neighbours told me, "Switch off your lights, there would be shelling", and when I came out of my house I saw people in shelters, and women and children were in shelters and I saw some people in uniform. All of a sudden, I realised how many people were carrying weapons and people whom I had never seen before with weapons carried arms. I was quite shocked to see all that. I was not afraid personally of my neighbours, but among those people in uniform there were many people with criminal records, people who had spent 10 or 15 years in prison, so there was a big risk. So that night, around 10 o'clock, I remember that Suljo Kusuran's group of people seized weapons from two JNA soldiers on the road to Prijedor/Banja Luka. My neighbours told me later on, Adil and Meho Beslagic, that they had seized one sniper and one automatic rifle. Those people went on to Prijedor and they informed their superiors, and that evening there was an order to give back the weapons otherwise Kozarac would be shelled. I was told that by Fikret who was standing in front of my cafe. His cousin told me that we should switch off the lights and that within the next 25 minutes something could happen. And I remember there was a black out. There was no public lighting, but I had no place to go. I did not know where I should go because, from some previous conversations with my neighbours, I saw that there was a list of shelters and my name was not there. My family was not on that list, and I did not know what could happen if there really is a shelling. So, in view of such circumstances, I did what I was told to do. I was standing in front of the cafe with Fikret and many people were hiding in shelters. There were vehicles passing by, vehicles that I had never seen before, camouflage colours, along Marsala Tita Street. There was no normal traffic any longer. People were carrying weapons, a lot of people. I do not remember seeing any civilian except for those who were in shelters. I remember I took a bottle of spirits to those people because I knew those shelters. I used to play there as a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you remain in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but that evening I said to myself, "I should leave, I should flee this town", because I realised that evening in case there is a conflict, I would stand no chance. I would have no chance to flee. So that evening I stayed in a cafe of my neighbour until midnight, with my neighbour Jakupovic, and then I went back home and that evening I slept in my cafe on a chair. I actually slept on the floor and I fell asleep. I do not remember whether I was really sleeping or not. Anyhow, that is how. Morning came and I did not know what had happened, but I heard that everything had been taken care of, and weapons that had caused the incident had been returned. But you never know, you never know whether something similar could happen once again. It was in the air. It was difficult to understand that such an incident over two rifles could bring about a war. But, anyhow, that evening I realised that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you decide then to leave Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you leave Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening I knew I should leave as soon as possible. I did not know when. The next morning when I saw that Relja Trivic's family was packing -- sorry, Trivo Reljic, Reljic Trivo is the man's name -- his family was packing and leaving Kozarac and I asked whether I could go with them and he said, "OK". I did not know what kind of situation was on the road Prijedor/Banja Luka, but after that incident there was a big question whether I could leave Kozarac at all. I spent the whole night thinking how I should leave the town, whether on foot. Then when I saw them packing, I thought that I could perhaps go with them. I did not have a car at that time. I did not have any friends in Kozarac who were not Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it only you living in the Tadic family home at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was alone. Well, for a long period of time I had changed the place I slept. When I came back to Kozarac it was -- it was difficult. I slept in my brother's part of the house. Sometimes I would sleep in our family house and sometimes I slept in the garage. I kept changing that because I was afraid. I was afraid that something might happen to me while I am asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who else was in Trivo Reljic's car when you decided to leave Kozarac with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agreed with him that we should meet in front of the house. It was just opposite my house. He was with his wife and his two sons. Before we left, I just took the register plates from my house. I am afraid that a similar thing might happen when we tried to leave Kozarac with the priest on 3rd May. That is why I suggested to him that I should go on foot and I did not want him to have the same problem. So, I set on along the Marsala Tita Street. I went that part of the road on foot because there were checkpoints there, military checkpoints, of the army from Kozarac. But I passed them and nobody told me anything. I waited for them on the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and they arrived in their car, zastava 750, and they then took me in their car. I know that before they arrived, an active policeman, Zijad Basic, left in his car. It was also a zastava one, a green zastava. He was living in Kozarac but he was working in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what time was this then that you left your house and went down Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember next to my house, the part which has been shown here several times, there is a restaurant and next to the restaurant there are several shops and several shops are across the street. I remember at that moment in the morning shops were being opened, so it could have been half past 8, 9 o'clock. I saw Mirka Kesic who was opening her shop and I also remember seeing Nasiha -- I think her family name is Susic -- and she was just opening a shoe shop. So it could have been around 8 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to taking a register. What do you mean by that, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is actually cashier from my cafe, and it was also a book like a ledger where you would enter all records of beverages and so. They have similar things in shops and it was used in my cafe. All other things that I had were quite too big, like a coffee machine or TV set, but it was all very heavy to carry. I did have some games, but they were all heavy to carry. So it was a very expensive thing and I remembered it so I took it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you moved from the house and you went down to the highway, did Trivo Reljic pick you up in his car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who else was in that car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His wife, his two sons and he. I know we were crammed in the car, but we left. I remember that before we left I had left my jacket because I did not want to leave the impression with the people who were on the road, the soldiers, that I was actually leaving Kozarac. So I took off my jacket and I only had a t-shirt on. It was a bright summer day. I was afraid that something would happen, something that I had felt previously, that I would be prevented from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to the checkpoint in Kozarac that you wanted to get through. Was that between your house and the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That checkpoint was in existence for a very long period of time. It was next to the veterinarian station and it was on the main road, not far from the Jela factory in Kozarac. But at that time when I arrived it was moved closer to the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so that we have this clear, was that before you actually get on to the highway itself? So if you turned off the highway and went into the main road in the direction of Marsala Tita Street, was the checkpoint in that section of road off the main highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just identify it briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you go along Marsala Tita Street in the direction of the main road, Prijedor/Banja Luka, the only street after you have passed my house that turns left in the direction of the church, so from that turn some 100 metres on the left there was a checkpoint with soldiers carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you remember to speak a little bit slower because the interpreters, I must stress, have to listen exactly to what you say and think in two languages and report it to us. So can you remember that, to speak slower? Perhaps if I go like that and move my hand, that is an indication to speak a little bit slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did the car of Trivo Reljic then pick you up after you had left Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 8 o'clock in the morning. As I said, around the period of time when the stores were opening in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I actually asked when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On May 23rd 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The car that picked you up, which direction did it travel in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were moving out of Kozarac in the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that on the new highway or the old highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were moving along the new highway Prijedor/Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you stopped during the course of that journey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We slowed down twice on the highway. The first time we thought that we would be stopped on the same road near the village of Koncari. That is where was that well-known Suljo Kusuran, "Kole", and he had stopped a military vehicle there and was controlling the documents. We used that moment and just sped up past that. The second time we slowed down at the checkpoint in Orlovci. We did not quite come to stop, but we slowed down and then we went on. I remember at the checkpoint Orlovci I saw there was a lot of military, and I recognised somebody I knew from before. There was Bogoljub Kovac. I think he had a moustache, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first place that you told us about involving slowing down where Kusuran, otherwise known as "Kole" was, how far from the point where you enter the new road from Kozarac was that first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you go from Kozarac to the new highway?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere -- I think there is about six kilometres distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went through ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six kilometres from Kozarac and about one kilometre, maybe two, to Orlovci. I think it is the last village with the Serb majority population, Koncari, as you move towards Kozarac from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that highway Prijedor/Banja Luka goes on to Bosanski Novi and on the same road, a couple of kilometres, and Reljic Trivo with his family stopped off so that I could get off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you get off the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the same road Prijedor/Bosanski Novi across from the railroad station and next to a store, I think it was the "Autoparts", the store that sells that, and I got off there, and they went on to the village of Svodna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how much time elapsed, somewhere, 8.00, 8.30, in Kozarac. It could have been 9.30. We were moving fairly slowly because it was an old vehicle and I do not know how much Trivo was using it, not much, some -- because of the fuel. I do not know if you know how zastava 750 looks like. It is a very small car and maybe it was 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you go in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that part of the road there is an unofficial railroad crossing, so I crossed it and I went into the street. I think the name of the street was Preradovica, I am not sure, but I went straight to Jelena Gajic who is my wife's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was she at home or at her place of work that you saw her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she was at home, both she and the children, also the mother of her husband was there and there were some neighbours. So there were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you stay there long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I stayed quite a while. I had a coffee. I had something to eat. I did not have time in Kozarac, so I was a bit hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What had happened to the cash register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cash register was small but pretty heavy, so I could not carry it, so it went with Trivo. I went in August of '93, so Trivo was keeping it in this village, Svodno, so later he gave it back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you stayed at Jelena Gajic's place for quite a while. Did there come a time when you left her place where she lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that there was a train to Banja Luka leaving around 12.00, so I went there. I told them about the circumstances of my leaving Kozarac. I managed to escape and that I was going to my family in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go down to the railway station and catch that train at Prijedor station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the train was already there and it was fairly full. There were people that I knew from before. They were people from Kozarac, from Prijedor. It was packed to capacity. Everybody was wondering if it was going to get going at all. Then around 12.00 we heard shells, so we were wondering whether it was going to get going. You could sense those shells flying over the city. The train started after 12.00, and we were all apprehensive, all the way through to Banja Luka, whether it would stop somewhere, it would arrive there, but we all made it to Banja Luka. I remember along the road it was a strange feeling. The tracks were going past the Serb and Muslim villages, but at the end when we got to Banja Luka we had a complete picture of what was going on behind us and it is something that stays in memory. As we were passing, for instance, through Trnopolje, I saw around crowds, people who were alongside the tracks with machine guns, with guns, and then you saw that they had the insignia of the Muslim army, of the Bosnian Army, and the same picture, the same script was in Serb villages, people lying around facing each other and facing the tracks, so that you could see the relationships that were going on at the time. In Ivanjska, that is where the Croats make a majority, they had different insignia, so everybody was armed. So on the train I saw different nationalities. So I think that most people around me felt like me. It did not matter which army would stop you, Serb or Muslim or Croat, and unload us. The train travelled very slowly. Finally, we got there. We stopped and alighted once, and we were thinking, we would wondering. There was a fear among people. The people were not talking much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did the train arrive in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 2.00 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On its way had it stopped at other stations between Prijedor and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the train would stop regularly, but once there were stop lights and it stopped but it would -- there were stations, Petrov Gaj, Trnopolje, Omarska, Ivanjska and Banja Luka. I think those are all the stations where the train stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Banja Luka where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only remember that at the exit I greeted Esad Tadzic who is a school friend of my brother. He used to be the President of the municipality in Prijedor. So he was with his wife. We greeted each other. We knew each other well. The families knew each other from before. We just shook hands. We said nothing that is interesting. There was silence, some apprehension and a very strange feeling. He grew up in Kozarac and lived in Prijedor, and I was born and grew up in Kozarac and we both ended up in Banja Luka. I assumed also that he had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So where did you go in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on foot to Starcevica settlement. I came to my brother and told him that I was alive, that I had just arrived from Prijedor and then I went to my family which lived in Koste Jarica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the place where you were staying in Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having arrived there, did you stay there or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there very briefly. I had a strange feeling and I thought that I had to go somewhere. There were several reasons for it. First, I wanted to take a bath. I wanted to eat. I wanted to relax and it was not possible in that house. It had almost nothing there. The food supplies and the money that my wife and my mother had was all spent during their period in Banja Luka. So the relationships were breaking down between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, and my mother was getting the pension from Belgrade and it stopped and so she had nothing left. They were without money. They had nothing. I had the daily intake from the cafe and that was it. So I suggested, I remembered my friend,[redacted], and we went there. I wanted to have a good meal and I knew that they were rich and I wanted to take a bath, so we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that you wanted to go there. How far away from the place where you were in Koste Jarica was the place where [redacted] lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite a while, quite a distance, five or six kilometres, the other side of town. It is a family house. It is on a transit road of a completely different part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go there with the rest of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole family came along and we went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would be your mother Staka, the two children and your wife Mira?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mother Staka, Mira and two children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you get to the [redacted] house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It took a while and we carried the younger daughter between us. She was three years then and my mother was not well. She had gangrene on her toe. So it was almost dusk when we arrived. It was already the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was at the [redacted] house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted] In other words, the family was there. Only he was living in one part of the house and in another one his brother with wife and mother lived in the other side. He only lived with his wife and daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how long did you stay in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not sure whether I was going to spend the night there. I was not thinking about it. I was not sure that he was going to keep me there. I did not know what was going to happen in the meantime, but [redacted] remained as he was before. So we spent the night and we left only the next evening, towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the house that they were living in a change from the place that you and your family were staying in in Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an exceptional house, very well appointed. The family [redacted] did not have money in the bank, but all the money that they were making, both he and his father, was invested into the house. [Redacted] [Redacted] So, they were quite well off. [Redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next day is 24th May 1992. At what time did you leave that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon, late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to our house where we were living in Koste Jarica Street. That was our reality, so we went back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The rest of that day, where did you spend that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent with my family thinking about what to do next. I tried -- I wanted my family to spend as little time there as possible because the conditions were terrible. So we were sitting in front of the house. There was always stench so you could never clean out that inside. There were some old things. I remember that for days and days we cleaned, and you just could not clean it out. So we were sitting in front of the house. Then I installed the antennae so that we had some conditions for living. We were planning what to do next and I said, "We will visit with friends, we will eat there, we will sleep here". We will try to find a job for my wife. That was the short term plan that we had. Other things we did not think about at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 24th May was the day that Kozarac was attacked. During the next five days did you go into Kozarac? Did you return to Kozarac at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the conflict in the Kozarac area, I did not go. The first information I heard on radio and television. I remember well that after about four or five days TV Banja Luka showed what was going on precisely in or around Kozarac. I remember Kotlovaca -- that is on Mount Kozara -- and they were showing -- that was where people went. They said that they -- the extremists burnt down a mountain lodge. Those were the first information -- that was the first information I saw on television. So, in a way I was following the news, mostly through television. They had their own view of events and I had left that town a few days ago, but the television had its own version of the truth. I remember well that they said that there was an agreement of sorts between the Crisis Staff and the Local Commune of Kozarac, that there was an agreement -- that there was an agreement between the two authorities that the buses would be sent to Kozarac by the authorities in Prijedor to take out civilians and that this was all part of the agreement between the Crisis Staff and the Local Commune authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first return to Kozarac, having left it on 23rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 1st June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about that period between those two dates of 23rd May and 1st June. How did you spend your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent my time with the family. For the most part, we cleaned the house. You just could not clean it out. That was one thing. On the other hand, in agreement with Jovo Samardzija, who was getting his pension in Banja Luka, I wanted to see that my mother was also receiving it there. She was registered in Prijedor municipality, so because she suddenly left the municipality she was cut off. So I went to the veterans' organisation. I had to open a bank account, and then had it forwarded to Belgrade. I registered my family with the Red Cross in Banja Luka. Then they were surprised how come there was a refugee from the Prijedor municipality. After an interview with the administrative worker at the Red Cross there, he said, "Yes, I will put you in with the refugees from Livno because so far nobody has reported from the Prijedor region. You are the first one". So we finally got a status. So that is the business that I finished until 1st June. Then we were visiting our friends. We visited with Nikola Petrovic, a long time friend. I have known him since the secondary school. He was going out with my wife's friend who was also a nurse. So we knew each other through those contacts. Also, he was an athlete, so we also met while we were training together. So we went there. We had lunch with him. After that we visited my uncle, Risto Vokic. I visited him primarily because we said that we were trying to find a job for my wife as a nurse in a hospital. He had some influence in Banja Luka. He said that he would see. We were all at his place and I remember he returned us in his car to Starcevica. He was at the time driving a zastava 101 model. So then we were dealing with trying to fix the house and visit with old friends, and pretty much on a daily basis I would go, if I went to my brother's, who had a business in the same settlement, Starcevica, in Milosa Duica Street, and then we would also often go to Jovo Samardzija. He was a long time friend of my father's and we would go there to have coffee and that kind of thing. Almost every night I was spending in my brother's company. At that time they were securing that area, that one part of that street and then another part, and I remember that on one occasion they did a silly thing. They put some tree trunks there and some policeman ran into it with his car, and so they were criticised. They were civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred there to a brother, which brother is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Ljubomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 1st June then is the first day that you returned to Kozarac. Did you go with anyone or were you by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
