utterances.text: From the moment when myself and my brother heard that the war operation in Kozarac area had stopped and you could find that out through the radio and newspapers, they said that the conflict was over, that the extremists had surrendered. In other words, they made it known that there was peace in the area, and my brother insisted that we go there. He had a store there and he had had a delivery of goods right before the war and that cost a lot of money. I was not eager. I was, kind of, disappointed but he always insisted day after day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that be your brother Ljubomir again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, for the most part, I spent time with him. He was living about a kilometre away and he was spending the time in that street, Milosa Duica, where I lived. He had his business there because he was living at his mother-in-law's and that was really an emergency residence, and he was spending time at his wife's place where she was with her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you travel to Kozarac then on 1st June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took a train.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went in the morning. I cannot recall, but they were running often, frequently, around 5.00 and 6.00, and I think that that was the only means of transportation that was used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which station did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first arrived in Omarska, the town of Omarska. Then we did not know what circumstances are, what the conditions are, in the area. We asked people and there were a lot of people wearing arms in the area. Mostly, people were talking about the events, that it was the war had started. Then we were asking around, what was the way to Kozarac? I did not know too many people in Omarska because there was never much communication between Omarska and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for going to Omarska railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no other way. The train stopped in Omarska and there was no other way to get to Kozarac. That was the only way. My brother had a car, but it was very risky to use it. It was a Ford which he had bought in Germany and there was always something amiss with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard that the railway station for Kozarac town is, in fact, at Trnopolje? Was there any reason why you did not go on the train to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not possible to go from Trnopolje to Kozarac. You would have had to walk for six kilometres. That was the only reason. In other words, it was much farther.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Going to Omarska then, what time did you get off the train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere maybe around noon we got to Omarska. Then we asked around what the conditions were, how we could get to the centre of Kozarac? Then some people pointed us in some kind of a headquarters, and we asked whether we could go to the place where we lived. They said it was not their authority; it was a regional Crisis Staff in Omarska. They called it headquarters or staff. It was really a one room where a uniformed officer was sitting and he said that the Kozarac was -- that in the Lamovita Crisis Staff is where we should find out about Kozarac. So we went there on foot and there, at least, I knew someone. I remember a waiter, Nenad Rakic, and I asked him, "Is there war in Kozarac?" He said, "No, no, it is all over, there are almost no people left". I was surprised, "How come?" He said, "Well, they were all evacuated". Then my brother and I went to the village, Timarci or Babici, I do not know what the official name is. That is where my waiter lived, Milenko Timarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that this would have come under the Lamovita Crisis Staff. Where was that situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in a Local Commune there. Previously -- I think it was the first time that I saw -- I visited a Local Commune there. It was like a youth centre there and they said, "This is where the regional Crisis Staff is which has authority over Kozarac. It is all -- Kozarac is part of that". I do not know. It was exclusively a military formation. I remember that there was a municipal Crisis Staff and then some people explained that now they had the absolute authority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see Milenko Timarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went to Timarac, to his house. We asked him, we said that we wanted to visit the house. He knew that I had a cafe, but he used to work there as a waiter but not the last six months. He agreed, and he said, "But you need a permit. You have to get a certificate for fuel", and then we agreed that I would look for that. So we went back to Lamovita. I went to the Local Commune because my brother was not officially registered there. I had a personal ID. I told them that I lived in Kozarac, and I told them that I am going to request them to go to Kozarac to visit my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to Lamovita and first of all saw Milenko Timarac, about what time was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was all around -- between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to the local Crisis Staff at Lamovita, what time would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, right after that we did that relatively fast. The village of Timarac is very close to Lamovita. It was all very quickly maybe. We left around 2 o'clock for Kozarac, not later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What vehicle did Milenko Timarac have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milenko had a zastava 101, white in colour. It was in a bad state of repair, but it served the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that a saloon car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a luxury car. I know that he used to live in Sisak, in Croatia, before the war, so he never changed his plates. It was always on his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that car were you able to travel into Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first we got the permit, I mean the certificate for the fuel. It was recorded somewhere and I know that the Secretary of the Local Commune, Drago Milencic issued me that. I met other people there and they told me that the Commander of the Crisis Staff there was Vinko Kos and he issued approval for me to get the fuel. So we went to the petrol station in Lamovita. We got the fuel and we went to Kozarac. We took the old Prijedor/Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you entered Kozarac were you able to pass into it without difficulty or were you stopped on the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a spot where they had some kind of control, unofficial control. It was in the direction of Kozarac when you leave Lamovita, but we stopped somewhere along the road and two more passengers joined us, Boza and Mirko Grahovac whom we knew from Kozarac. They were coming from the village of Lukici. They were also going to Kozarac on foot. So we gave them a lift and we arrived in Kozarac together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you were stopped at a point. Who was running that point? Who controlled that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, honestly, I do not know. It was a person in uniform, half uniform, half civilian clothes. He had an M48 rifle and there were some other villagers standing with him. They were not really organised and there was an obstacle on the road, a tree trunk. That is why I am saying it was an unofficial checkpoint. They did not know what they really wanted when they stopped us. They did not ask us anything. They just asked us where we were going. I told them that we were going to Kozarac and they said, "OK, you can go to Kozarac".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you visit the family home on this occasion of 1st June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Before I visited the house on the road next to the church where there used to be a checkpoint Grahovac and his wife got out, and they went to their family house and we went to the centre of the town to our family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you get to the Tadic family house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been about 3.00 o'clock, 3.00 p.m. I know that we had been, that we were travelling for about one hour, hour and a half. We just drove through Kozarac, the three of us. We went to -- I remember we went in the direction of the fire station. Then we went back when we saw what was happening there, what had happened there, that a lot of it had been destroyed. So we went back to the factory, Jela factory, and that is where I saw an acquaintance of mine. It all lasted very short because when we went back Kozarac was in a pitiful shape. It was not so much destroyed, but there was a stench in the air. There was no electricity at that time. So later on in my house I saw in my freezer that all the food that I had had been spoiled, there was some cattle around. It was difficult to explain such a feeling, but you could feel something in the air, you could feel that something was unhealthy in the air. We did not see many soldiers. I saw several people, that was all. All along the road I just saw that unofficial control near Lamovita and later I did not see anyone when we were going there or when we were coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in the area of Kozarac on this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one hour, an hour and a half. We wanted to do something useful. My brother wanted to do something about his business premises. He wanted to protect something. I tried to shut down the area because everything was laying open and things were scattered around. So I first established the situation. So during that first visit to our family house we realised that the house had not been really destroyed but the front part of the house where there were business premises of my brother, there was a huge opening, a huge hole of maybe a shell. The part of the house where I had been sleeping for several months, that is the part of the house that belongs to my brother Mladen, there was a hole in the roof which had been made by a shell, and a shell had fallen in front of the house and damaged the terrace. So it was quite a pitiful shape. My cafe was damaged. Everything was more or less damaged. It was a rather sophisticated kind of interior in the cafe. So when windows were smashed and doors were smashed, everything was just laying open. The town itself was ghostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had anything been removed from either your house or your cafe premises or Ljubo's business premises so far as you could tell on this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time. Well, I did not check details. I did not really think about that. I just saw that most of the valuable equipment in my cafe was OK. So that the coffee machine was damaged, but it was still usable. The TV set was still there because I had two TV sets, one in my house where I was living and the other in the cafe, in my business premises. I had two games machines. Most of it was OK. The property had been damaged, but it was still usable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take anything with you from the house when you left it after this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took only, as far as I can recall, my stereo chain, the one I was using in my cafe. It is very expensive equipment. I spent DM4,500 on that. So I thought I should take that. I put it in Milenko's car although he protested, but I could not take anything else except for that. It did not take up too much space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A stereo chain, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is it, that is a musical equipment stereo system without musical boxes, without loud speakers, they were too big to carry. I remember I left that with Milenko Timarac in his house and that equipment stayed in his house for quite a while. I do not remember when I took it to my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Milenko Timarac's house? What time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late in the afternoon, very late. I do not recall what time it was, but I know we did not stay too long in Kozarac. There was an incident in the street with my brother and it was quite unsafe. We were there as civilians. Milenko warned us, he told us that we should not stay there too long. Then it was not difficult when you were wearing civilian clothes, if people see you wearing civilian clothes. There was a chaos in the street at that time. There were very old men in uniforms, men aged 75 and young men as young as 18. The situation was rather awkward and as a civilian it was not wise to walk around the street. My brother had a kind of incident at that time, and the person warned us. He told us it was still an area under military operations. I forgot to say that in addition to the cash register, I took my hunting rifle and my other rifle from the house, after the warning of this officer who told us it was quite risky to move around. Before that incident we did not have any weapons with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred then to the cash register. As I understood your evidence, you told us that the cash register was taken when you left Kozarac on 23rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The weapons that you have referred to, did you take them on the 23rd May or the visit on 1st June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 1st June. On 23rd May I did not have any weapons with me. Even the handgun that I had for which I had a permit was not there. I had left it with my wife in Banja Luka because during her stay in Banja Luka the place was attacked two times. A window was smashed and they wanted to rob the house. So once after I had left the gun with my wife, she was keeping the gun although she could not really handle it, she was not strong enough. So I left it with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about weapons. What weapons did you own at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after 1985 I filed a request, an application, and I was allowed and consequently I bought a gun, a 765, zastava make, and I kept it at home mostly. Except for that weapon, my brother who had spent the last four months of 1991, my brother Mladen, he stayed in Kozarac quite a few times. He had some problems with his wife in Munich. So he tried to come back and live in Kozarac. That was his idea. He was in the process of building his business premises, so he would spend a long time in Kozarac with his daughter. Because he was a hunter he brought a hunting rifle and that hunting rifle was always in the house. He was the owner of the hunting rifle. At the end of 1991 I got an automatic rifle from a deserter whose name was Mile Kusota.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The hunting rifle that you referred to then which belonged to Mladen, did you take that from the house on 1st June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did take it with me, but it was useless. It used to be a very expensive rifle. He had bought it in Munich. It cost him between DM6,000 and DM7,000. It had some decoration on it as far as I can remember. So I took it, although I could not really use it. You could take it apart, so it was quite safe. Children could not use it. Even adults who did not know how to use it could not really use if they did not have the mechanism which I kept always apart. It was not in my house, but when my brothers were not in Kozarac I was using their parts of the house and I was keeping an eye on it. So his rifle was always there in his part of the house. So I took apart that mechanism, firing mechanism, from the rest of the rifle and I could not find that mechanism. It had disappeared. Someone had taken it away. I think that it was gold plated, that mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The automatic rifle you told us about that you had got at the end of 1991, did you take that away on 1st June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take both of those weapons to Lamovita with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first we went to Milenko's house where I left the hunting rifle because it could not be used anyway, and I took the automatic rifle with me to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time then did you leave Lamovita to continue your journey to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we did not go to Lamovita. I do not know whether I mentioned that. Milenko, from his house there are two roads. The village of Timaraci is between the road, the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and the old Prijedor/Banja Luka road, somewhere in the vicinity of the village of Jakupovici. So there are several roads that you can take if you want to go to the main Prijedor/Banja Luka road from that village. So he took us along a village road, a village street, which joins the main road somewhere after Kamicani. So he took us there and he took us in his car to the junction Lamovita/Omarska road and Prijedor/Banja Luka road. There is a junction there and there is a petrol station there on the right-hand side, and that is where we waited for about 15 minutes. So after we arrived in the village of Timaraci we did not go back to Lamovita. That is what we did when we were coming to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So where did you go having finished your business in Timaraci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We hitchhiked a vehicle and went to Banja Luka. I believe it was a lorry. I know that Milenko Timarac waited with us until we left because he was not sure that we would be able to leave. At that time there was no bus service functioning and he said, "I will wait with you if you manage to leave OK. If you do not you can come back to my place and stay overnight", but we left. It could have been around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. We had been waiting for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you return to the place where you were staying in Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having visited Kozarac on this occasion, when did you next return to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have to mention that when we came back to Banja Luka, I know that my brother told me at that time that we should have a uniform, and we were wondering because it was difficult to move around without a uniform. So he gave me a uniform because it was quite difficult to move around the town itself, let alone leave Banja Luka. So I stayed there for a while, very briefly, and then I left for our family house where we were living at that time in Koste Jarica Street and I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you next return to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was after the visit to Trnopolje and before my mobilization in the reserve police force. I cannot recall the exact date. I could guess, but I know when I visited Trnopolje and I know when I was mobilized. I know that this visit took place in between, roughly between the 8th, 9th or 10th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us deal first of all then with the visit to Trnopolje. When did take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The visit took place on Saturday, 6th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the conflict ended and after my brother and I visited our family house in Kozarac, Jozo Samardzija kept insisting, asking that someone should go with him to Trnopolje because he had met some people from Kozarac in Banja Luka and he had heard that many people from Kozarac were in Trnopolje and that his sister was among them. She used to live in the village of Kamicani before. So he kept asking us every day. At the beginning I kept refusing and my brother refused too. So my brother said that I should do it. He was an old man and he needed, he insisted that we helped him. That is why I accepted. Although I visited him several times and I told him, "OK, I am ready" or "I can go now", and then he said he would not feel very well. So that is how we met, at least four or five times before we went, and it was all after the military operations, after the conflict was over. So we postponed the visit several times. Then that weekend I told him", "Well, if you do not want to go today I am not going to go", so he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the day that you went was it just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just the two of us. That morning I talked to my brother and I told him that I had accepted to go. I told Jovo that he should get ready. Then I went home, took my weapon, my uniform and came to get Jovo who was waiting for me in the street and that is how we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what time did you leave then to go to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you travel from Banja Luka to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we went on foot from Starcevica to the railway station. It is very far from Starcevica, five or six kilometres, and since he is an old man he walked very slowly and with difficulty. Then we went to the railway station, Banja Luka, and we took a train to Trnopolje. I think we arrived in Trnopolje around 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Trnopolje did you realise at that time where the collection centre or camp was located in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the railway station where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the centre of Trnopolje where the Local Commune should have been or what used to be the centre of the village. It is the road Trnopolje/Kozarac or vice versa, the main road. We got there and the usual thing is to ask in a cafe. So we went to a cafe in the centre of the town. I do not know whether it was Hilmo's cafe. Anyway, we asked and we realised that there were some people there from the Red Cross and some soldiers as well. So we talked to them and they wanted to see our identification cards which we showed to them. We told them who we were, where we had come from and Jovo explained whom he was looking for. They said there were no problems, that he can go and look for that person. So we stayed there for about an hour, maybe an hour and a half, not more than that. We just stayed there for an hour. For most of the time we were just waiting for the train at the railway station and we were coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How were you dressed on this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wearing civilian clothes underneath, jeans and a t-shirt, and the uniform that my brother had given to me is like an overall, it is a kind of uniform, but the one that you wear on top of another uniform. The colour is that of a camouflage type. I know it was yellow in colour and spotted yellow and brown. It was a very thin uniform that you can easily put on your normal clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take any weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had the automatic rifle with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go up to the site of the former school in Trnopolje and where the cinema was, the hall, and visit the place of the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that moment I did not know what the collection centre was, and I did not know about the division that I have heard about here. Jovo and I met people whom we knew from before. Many people, many neighbours knew me. They did not know Jovo but I talked to them. We greeted each other, kissed each other. I remember seeing Ferid Gujnic in the street, Osman Turkanovic. We kissed each other. They were curious to know what was going on. I asked them what had happened because I was surprised to find them there. They had been living in the centre of Kozarac and all of a sudden they were there. I had heard on the news in Banja Luka that people were being transported and all of sudden I saw my neighbours in Trnopolje. Then I asked them, "Well, what will you do?" They asked me what was going to happen, and I just could not give them any answer. People gathered around me. They wanted to know what would happen and I told them I did not know. Anyhow, I knew there was a war going on. That is what I told Ferid. I remember seeing my neighbour Refko, a barber. All of a sudden I was called by Zujic Mujo who was a paramedic who used to work in the hospital before the war with my wife. So he called my name. He was standing there at the spot where a surgery was and that is where I also saw Jusuf Pasic, a doctor. They were wearing white doctors' uniforms. I also saw my former waiter Goga who was wearing a white coat. I had a coffee with them. They prepared something. Mujo wanted absolutely that we should have a cup of coffee. So we had a cup of coffee and Mujo asked me -- I knew that he had been born in Banja Luka and that he was living in Banja Luka for a long period of time. He was only married in Kozarac. When he heard that I was in Banja Luka and that I was going back on the same day, he said that he would give me his brother's address and he wanted me to tell his brother where he was. So he wrote his brother's name and his address on a piece of paper, his address in Banja Luka, and I promised that I would pay him a visit and that I would tell him where he was. I remember I had a long conversation with Osman Turkanovic there, because his sister used to work as a nurse with my wife before the war. So I asked him how he was. He said that he would be leaving soon and things like that. It all happened very quickly. Jovo was with me all the time. He was walking around asking people where his sister was. Then he said that he heard that his sister had left. Then I asked, "But what happened to those people? Where did they leave to Zenica?" They said they left in convoys to Zenica. That was one of the first convoys used for transportation of people. Those people were supposed to go to Banja Luka, but apparently, and such was the information, the police in Banja Luka would not allow them to get off the train in Banja Luka. So the train went on in the direction of Zenica. At that moment Jovo did not exactly know what had happened with his sister. So the first information we received was several days after when we were in Banja Luka. Rekko's wife, Sabiha Fazlic, told him about what happened, she is from Kozarac. She said that she was in Banja Luka on the same train with his sister. She said that the train had slowed down and people were supposed to get off, but the police were shooting and they did not allow the train to stop. So she jumped off the train, but his sister could not jump because she was an old woman. So that is how she ended up in Zenica. Jovo later on enquired about her with the Red Cross, and then later on he managed somehow to get in touch with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what time did you actually leave Trnopolje from the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not later than 3.00 p.m. We stayed there for about an hour talking to those people standing in the street mainly, and when we realised there was no point in waiting we left. I remember that I caught some -- I found some cigarettes and gave them to those people. I remember giving some cigarettes to an old friend of mine Kulasic Sahib. I am not a smoker, but we asked some other people for cigarettes and we gave them to those other people. I told them that I could not find cigarettes for them. I remember we talked to a lady. There is a house next to the railway station and Jovo was talking to that woman. He was asking about his sister. So he spent sometime, a long time, I do not know how long, maybe half an hour, an hour. We were sitting there in front of the railway station waiting for the train. I believe we were the only passengers at that moment from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive back in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 4.00 o'clock, 5.00 p.m. I cannot tell you the exact time, but it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (Luncheon Adjournment).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about the second visit to Kozarac in this period when you were living in Banja Luka. First of all, why did you make another visit to Kozarac during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first time we saw that our family house was filled with precious things that we wanted to evacuate from there. There were large quantities of drinks that my brother Ljubomir brought to his discount, and at first there were still things in my house that I wanted to rescue, plus in my residence I had my clothing. Everything I had remained there. That was the only reason for us to go back to Kozarac again. There was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long after the visit to Trnopolje that you have told us about was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought about it a long time, and I am really sure now that it happened, I think, that we were in Trnopolje on Saturday, Sunday. Together with my brother we visited Mujo Zujic's brother in Mala Carsija. I told him where his brother was in Trnopolje, and then the next day, the following day, we went to Kozarac. So it could have been Monday, 8th or 9th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this occasion did you visit Kozarac on your own or were you with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I always moved around with my brother. I was not mobilized then, and it was not good to move around without papers. My brother was known around Banja Luka. So, in any event, had I been arrested, it would not have been that dangerous because at that time during my stay in Banja Luka it was dangerous to move about the city. There were some groups in all key locations. If you passed across the bridge of the River Vrbas, the bus would be stopped. There would be controls. People were off loaded or people would go in and there was general chaos in the city. Both in the city and wherever else I went, I went with my brother, never by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave Banja Luka on this occasion of the second visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon, as far as I can recall. We also took the train to Omarska, to the railway station in Omarska. Then we took the same road and went to the village of Babici or Timarci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who did you see in that village at Timarci or Babici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first went on foot to the junction of the road Lamovita/Omarska and Banja Luka, that was the main road, and I remember a van passed -- it was not a van, it was a military jeep type of vehicle -- and they gave us a lift to the vicinity of that village. We arrived there in the afternoon into Timarci. I found Milenko Timarac. I know it was pretty late. He said that we should stay with him, so we agreed and we stayed. We stayed in his house. There was his father, mother and brother and wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you stay overnight with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We stayed the whole night. I remember they had night watchers at the entrance of their house. They were telling stories about that they did not take part in the attack of Kozarac, that they were defending their village, that one of the people in the village was killed. There was a shell that fell in the vicinity and he died of a heart attack. He was -- Milenko's father also knew my father well and he respected him before the war, before this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next day then, which would have been a Tuesday, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not go to Kozarac right away. We thought that everything was as usual, as before. We met a few people and they said, "Don't worry, nothing will be touched in your house". When we were first in the house we saw some signs, "This is Serbian", because a lot of people who were taking part in this knew about the house, so there were signs "Don't touch", and such. We ourselves thought that everything would be all right, that nobody touched anything there. So, at first we did not go to that house right away. We were looking for a truck. That is, Milenko took us to Omarska and we found a truck there. We made a deal with a private truck driver. I know that it was a private truck businessman. He had a truck business before the war. So we did not go right away, maybe an hour or two we stayed, and then when we arrived we realised that the house was not in the condition we left it in at the time of the first visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just stop you here and get some timings? Do you know when it was that you left Babici or Timarci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what time in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in the morning, I do not exactly recall. I never wore a watch on me, so .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you get from Timarci down to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Pile's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is "Pile" another name for Milenko Timarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is Milenko Timarac also known as "Pile", and he was known as "Pile" because he had a chicken farm before the war in Croatia broke out. "Pile" means "chicken" in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to Omarska where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the marketplace, that is, the livestock market which is in the central part of town. Milenko knew some truckers and he brought over a man and he said, "Why don't you make a deal?" I know that my brother paid for this because I did not have the money, and I remember that it was 50 deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the trucker that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I saw him for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you did not know him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not know people in Omarska. I had no business there. That is why we asked Pile to come with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you made the arrangement with the trucker, what time was it that you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say, but I think around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Leaving Omarska with the trucker, was that you and your brother Ljubomir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself, my brother Ljubomir and this trucker, and we went to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 1 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived on this occasion in Kozarac, did you go straightaway to the family home in Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the family home, was it in the same condition as it had been the few days before when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that when we were going from Omarska to Kozarac we were taking the highway, the main road. After Kamicani, we took the old road. So, we passed by the church and came to the centre of Kozarac. So, it was not in the same condition. It was very different -- not only my house; I saw that many things changed. Along the road we saw smoke rising from houses. They were burning -- I had not seen that before -- and the house was pillaged. Many things were missing from there. What I saw in my cafe, and I mostly wanted to come to Kozarac for the cafe, because all the things of value were there, they were new things -- it had only be opened for about a year -- there was almost nothing evident. Whatever could have been -- could be taken away was taken away. The interior was made in such a way that you could dismantle things. My brother and myself dismantled the ceiling part and then there were some marble parts that we could take down. My brother thought that he would find his crates of beer still full, but he found nothing. Mostly, it was his crates and that ceiling. I found a few -- some glassware and there were no alcoholic drinks at all left, even though I had large supplies before the war. I had hard liquor and I had others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the family home on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe two hours at the most, so we were in a hurry. We did not stay long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you load up the truck with any property from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my brother as far as his valuables were concerned, he was only able to load up those empty crates that were -- it was a mid-sized truck, and my effects were taking up the smallest part. It was all -- it was mostly the ceiling construction and some parts of the bar. That was mostly it. I also found some, not so much clothing, but some bedding, some linens, in the house which I had not managed to take out before. So there was not much that we could take with us which was of value, which was worth taking. Had I known what the condition the house would be in, I never would have gone there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave Kozarac on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During that period whilst you were there, did anything happen that sticks out in your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Kozarac was -- the centre of Kozarac had not changed that much. The truth is I was not looking around much. When I went upstairs in my house the other roofs seemed intact. For the most part, it seemed intact, Kozarac was not destroyed. It mostly looked bad because it was abandoned, so it looked -- we could see children's clothing hanging on clothes lines around the houses. We saw livestock as they wander about. It was just a bad impression, but I could see few soldiers. Sometimes somebody would pass by, but they would be people that I saw for the first then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any civilians in Kozarac at this time whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was the family Coprka, Stoja and Drago, because they are exactly at the corner of the Orthodox church, and Mirko Grahovac and his wife. I saw no other inhabitants, even though at the centre of Kozarac Muslims and Croats and Serbs all lived there, but now it was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take all those goods that you had got from the family home back to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that on the same truck that you had hired in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive back in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was already dusk when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this period were you mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this period had you taken part in any of the cleansing activities, as they are called, in that area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw anybody there. When I got to Kozarac, during the first visit or second visit, there was nobody there. I did not know what was going on around there, but in the centre of Kozarac I saw no one except for these two families that I mentioned. The first time Grahovac came with us and the second time there were only those two families that lived in Kozarac. I do not know if anybody else lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When, in fact, were you mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mobilized exactly on -- I reported on 15th July 1992, and the mobilization was June 16, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at what I have seen on transcript here, it says you were "mobilized exactly on -- I reported on 15th July and the mobilization was on June 16, 1992". When did you report for your mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported on 15th June to the office -- not July, June -- and then I was mobilized on 16th June. That was my first day on duty. It was Monday when I reported. In fact, at first I was not paying attention. I was not sure whether 15th was the day of mobilization or 16th because the procedure was such that I was not fully aware of it. Afterwards, when I looked at my military booklet, my first day of duty was June 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were mobilized on this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw first that there would be problems with mobilization when I reported my family to the Banja Luka Red Cross. I also wanted to report myself as a refugee, but that -- I could not do that. There were already some laws passed that I was not aware of. I had never been in the reserves. I had never been part of any military exercise. So I did not know the procedure, how things were done. But in the Red Cross they told me, "No, there is no way, you cannot report. First, you have to report to the military office and then they will determine your status". That is when I reported my family there. Then they said, "You first have to report to the military", and that was in Prijedor. I had to report there. Besides, during that period of time in Banja Luka, I met Vokic Radovan, my cousin. I asked him -- I met him twice and once in the city, in town, and on the street -- and I asked him, "Can I get mobilized? Can I when I want so that I do not go to the military?" He said, "You have to join something, whether the military or somewhere, or else you will be arrested", and that is what was going on. There were instances when people were arrested, especially if people had certain mobilization locations in their military booklets, because in May and June they had -- they would call up people, that there were mobilizations. So, everybody who had their location had to report. So, I did not have that. In 10 years I was doing private business. I was moving around often, and that was for the military office. That was inconvenient because they could not follow my movements, plus I did not know the full procedure in order to be at the military's disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So to which body were you eventually mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mobilized in the reserve police force. As I said, I met Radovan Vokic and I asked him if he could help me. He was an active policeman and I found out that I had to report to the military office either in Prijedor or in Banja Luka. I did not want to go back to Prijedor. I thought that I would settle my affairs in Banja Luka, that I would find a job for my wife. At that time you could leave a certain residence only with permission of the military. Vokic promised that he would do something, that he would talk to the police Commander. I know that my brother put in a word for me. Vokic and myself were not very close, but we were family and he said that I should come, and I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which brother was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is always Ljubomir when I talk about Banja Luka. I had an older brother, Stojan. He was also never mobilized. He was hiding all the time, and up-to-date he has not been mobilized for some -- in some way he was able to avoid this. Precisely because of that I know that this older brother was arrested in Banja Luka, so Ljubomir had to go and get him out. It was also a rule that if one of the brothers was on the frontline, then the others did not have to go. So the authorities had some kind of understanding in those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The period you are talking about when you met Radovan Vokic and there was discussion about your mobilization, how long before 16th June did that occur? Can you give us an idea of the time? Can you also speak slowly as I know that the interpreters are having difficulty keeping pace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second meeting in Banja Luka took place after our arrival and the evacuation of our things from Kozarac and the mobilization itself. The next time I met Vokic was in my uncle's apartment, Risto Vokic's apartment, and he promised once again he would do anything so that I would be accepted in the reserve force of the traffic police. So I was trying to be mobilized in a unit which had nothing to do with the war whatsoever which would not take part in the war operations. I knew from before that traffic police did not take any part in war operation, nor was it planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you talk about the traffic police, in which town would that traffic police be based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My obligation, as I told you, I had to be mobilized in the Prijedor municipality. That was the only possibility, either the military or the police. There was not a third possibility. So, when I speak about the police, I speak about the Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did there come a time when you travelled to Prijedor to take up your mobilization with the reserve traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Prijedor on Monday. I was met there by Vokic in front of the police building. He took me to the centre of the Prijedor police, and I remember that on that day I first met Duro Prpos, and before that I met with Dusan Jankovic who was the chief of the police at that time. So we first had to talk to him. He had to give his permission. He asked me why I had not taken part in the war, where I had been at that time. He was rather angry with me and Vokic said, "Well, let it go, there will be enough time for that". So he tried to explain to me that I had been in a very difficult situation, and I know that Jankovic accepted my mobilization quite reluctantly, and I know that on that occasion I also met Stevo Lazic who also worked with the Prijedor police. After that conversation with Jankovic, though, he gave his approval for my being mobilized in the police and I insisted to be mobilized in the traffic police. Then Vokic introduced me to Djuro Prpos and Djuro Prpos said, OK, he needed people and that is how I was accepted in the reserve force of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On Monday, 15th June, at what time did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you travel from Banja Luka to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By train.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect at what time you arrived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left very early, I think it was before 6 o'clock in the morning. So I arrived in Prijedor before 7.00. I remember that the opening hours of the office was around 7 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was your first day of duty in the reserve traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was on duty on 16th June 1992 in Orlovci on the Prijedor/Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage your family was still in Banja Luka, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were still in Banja Luka, but before my departure for Prijedor, before my mobilizations, we knew, we were aware, that we could not have any status in Banja Luka. My wife received an answer that she could not find a job in Banja Luka and that she had to report in Prijedor for a job. So if you were not either mobilized in the police or the military, you could not have any status at all. You could not have any rights whatsoever. So each employee had to bring a kind of certificate that his or her spouse was either mobilized either in the police or in the military. Mobilization was the criteria for all the rights and the status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you travelled to Prijedor on Monday, 15th June, was that you on your own or were your family with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled alone to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage did you have any accommodation or any place to stay in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have anything, I did not know. At first I did not know whether I would be mobilized in the traffic police or regular police or somewhere else. I was not quite sure, and I did not even know whether I would be mobilized in the unit which suited me. So, the situation was quite uncertain for me. I did not know what would happen. So that evening when I arrived on 15th, I know that I spent the night at Radovan Vokic's place. He left his address. He said that he would be there for a certain period of time. So, because I did not have any address, so they asked me for something. So I spent the night in his flat in the Pecani neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the only night that you spent at his flat or did you spend other nights there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only night I spent at his place. I did visit him several times later on, but that was the time when I spent a night at his place. Vokic was absent very often. He was always away on business, travelling, whether in Banja Luka or elsewhere, so that is why I did not want to stay there overnight and my wife was alone at home, so I did not quite like -- I did not feel like being there alone. That is why I would sleep when I had to stay overnight with Martin and Mileva Dzaja at their place. It is an old couple, and it was much easier for me to stay overnight at their place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when accommodation was given to you in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, between 20th or on 21st or 22nd June 1992 I visited Prijedor town hall and there was a clerk there and I asked him for accommodation. I said I was working for the Prijedor police. It was a kind of condition, a requirement, for accommodation. So I showed him my booklet which testified that I had been mobilized, and I discussed with people from the Crisis Staff. He referred me -- he sent me to the Pecani neighbourhood and he told me that there is a commission in charge there. He said that I would find an apartment there. He did not give me an exact address, but he said that those people in that commission were in charge of making lists of apartments available so that I should see with them. That is what I did. I went to Pecani and I was looking for those people for sometime. I did not know exactly where they were, but then I found out and I found them at Pecani No. 2, building No. 2, B2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you eventually given a flat by the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I got into that flat there were three members of the commission sitting there and they were making, kind of, a list of the inventory that they had found in the flat. I told them I had a paper, a certificate, from the municipality which said that I had no accommodation and that I should be helped. I told them what the problem was. They said, OK, they just had to register all the property that was there. At that time the flat was already half empty, but whatever there was I had to sign for it. There was a kind of a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you given that flat on a temporary or a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was never really given that flat. They told me I should call back and they told me to sign the paper and I signed it. So, the first decision, written decision, that I received was at the beginning of 1993. I realised at that time that the flat was not on my name. What it says was only "Hasan Tulundzic" and January was the first month that I had to pay the rent for. So I had to pay the rent on his behalf as well as the utilities, and that is what I did. Nothing was really on my name, so at that moment I realised that the flat was not on my name and I was not familiar with the regular procedure, and I did not know how it should have been done. I did not think about whether I should make an official request to have the apartment officially allocated to me. So, that was never really done, but they knew I was living there by the very fact that I later on received an order to move out and the address was there in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your family eventually move into that flat and did you all start living there in Pecani, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I first brought my wife from Banja Luka to Prijedor and she spent two days cleaning up the apartment. She packed some things. I do not know how, but she managed to get in touch with the cousin of the owner of the flat, with the previous owner of the flat. I think she contacted her by telephone. So they made an agreement that she should pack certain things and send them to her. So I remember that my wife just spent those two days packing things. She was looking for some clothes and things like that. So she had finished in those two days and I remember I helped her. So the last day we were packing things, I remember I found a vehicle and we loaded all the things in that vehicle and took those things to that woman who lived near the hospital in Prijedor. I know they were looking for some other things as well. There was a table that she wanted, some flower pots, palm trees, very big, but she said that she had no place for that so she said that it can remain. It could remain in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what was the date, it you can remember it, or how long after you started your mobilization was it that you moved into the flat in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved in on 27th June 1992. My wife had come earlier and I had already had a key as of 20th, but we moved in after we had tidied up the place. So we arrived very early by train from Banja Luka, my wife, my children and my mother. I met them at the railway station in the morning and we went to the apartment in Pecani and we were living there as of that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Martin Dzaja whom you mentioned, how often did you stay at his place until you moved into the flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent three or four nights at his place. The first time it was with my wife, I think it was -- I believe on 17th June. It was the second day of my duty. I spent that night at Dzaja Martin's place with my wife. I had gone to pick up my wife and I brought her there. When I arrived, I learned that in the hospital in Prijedor they had issued some kind of declarations at that time. You had all kind of strange laws at that time. Everything was in relation with the mobilization and things like that. So, because my wife had worked in Kozarac before, I learned that it was a kind of declaration whereby by 20th June all those who wanted to work should report to their workplace, and that is why I went to fetch her and I brought her to Prijedor, otherwise she would have lost the job for ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you were given the key on 20th June. Were you staying at the flat before your family came to live there on 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. I slept at Martin and Mileva's place for a couple of nights. I do not remember exactly how many. The first time, as I told you, was with my wife when she came to Prijedor. We went there together. After that, I spent several nights at their place on my own. I know that Martin was always there, and his wife would go to sleep to her neighbour, a Muslim woman, who was afraid to be alone, whose husband had died some time before, and that was the reason why he was alone also. So it was OK with him. He was always a bit afraid of weapons, and I would leave my weapon when I was not on duty at his place. He was a little bit afraid because he was a Croat and he was afraid that he might be arrested if anyone should find that weapon at his place. But, anyhow, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that Martin Dzaja was a Croat. Was he an old family friend of the Tadic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had known each other for a very long time. We knew each other through my wife's sister. He was the uncle of the sister of my wife. Anyhow, they were related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is he an old man? Do you know what age he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he is an old man. Well, maybe he is 70, 70 years of age, maybe more. He is very sick and he looks much older. He was retired very early. He had worked in a factory, in a food factory, and I had known him for very long and we were on very good terms all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When your family moved to Prijedor, did you continue to work within the reserve traffic police at the checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never stopped working. I was working from 16th June and I had regular duties and I always went to work and I was never absent from work. It was like a job because it was paid and I think the traffic police was the only force that was, whose members were being paid. That was one of the main -- that was the main reason why I worked there. It was our only source of money at that time because my wife could not get a job right away, although she reported on time. So I managed to register my mother in Banja Luka with the war veterans' association because we thought we would stay there, but then we moved to Prijedor. So again I had to repeat the whole procedure and my brother helped me. So we had to cancel residence in Banja Luka and report again in Prijedor. So throughout that period she never received any pension. She did not receive pension until September. So that was our main source of income.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did your wife eventually get a job in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She got a job actually twice. At the beginning of August I think she was offered a job, but she refused to work. I went to the hospital to have some talks with people there, because she was given a job in a psychiatric asylum which was very difficult and it did not suit her and she did not want to work with mental patients. So some weeks passed in the meantime, and then I went again and I asked people again and she was eventually accepted in the Prijedor -- to work in the Prijedor hospital. I know the manager was Ljuban Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were doing your duties at Orlovci for the reserve traffic police, did you work as part of a unit of three policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were the names of the other policemen who were in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duty -- the shift Commander, Commander of my shift, was Miroslav Brdar and my colleague was Miroslav Cvijic. So the three of us worked together on the same shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know either of those men before you started working with them on 16th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have looked in this courtroom at duty lists showing the times that you were working at the Orlovci checkpoint as well as the dates. Did you miss any days of work that you should have undertaken at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I was never absent. We all paid much attention to that because, first of all, we did not want and never occurred to us to make a simple mistake in our work because it was very easy for us to be removed from such a post. We all cared, we all cared a lot, about working in the traffic police. So, if people were absent, it means that they were again -- they could be easily mobilized because at that time there were a lot of war operations going on in the area of Gradacac. So people who worked for the traffic police were lucky that they were working there because they knew that they would not be sent to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard that the Commander of the reserve traffic police was Djuro Prpos. As a Commander who controlled the reserve traffic police, what sort of discipline did he have with those policemen who worked under him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was very strict. I was not accustomed to such kind of discipline, military discipline, because I had never been in the reserve, because I did not know what it meant. Even when I was doing my regular military service, I did not have any special, any particular obligations, any particular training in relation with discipline. So I was not quite familiar with the way things functioned there. But Djuro Prpos was a professional, first of all. We were all reserve policemen and he was the only professional there. So he knew what he wanted. He was very strict, yes. I did not know him before, so I did not have any idea of what kind of a man he was. He himself was very disciplined, very strict. We did not have any private talks. We would run into each other in the town and greet each other, but there was a certain distance between us. I never had a chance to have a drink with him or a coffee. During that time I simply never had an opportunity for that. He was keeping a distance with us. He was strict, very strict. We accepted that because we knew that it was better for us that way. He behaved towards us as an active policeman. We had a similar treatment. We were receiving a salary which was quite adequate, given the circumstances. You could live on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We heard from a lady called Radoslavka Lukic that she lived near the checkpoint at Orlovci, and your brother Ljubomir pointed the lane near the tree that took you to her house. Did you have any contact with her whilst you were working at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had known her from before, from the elementary school, and when I arrived in Orlovci I did not know who her husband was and I did not know where she lived, but when I arrived there I saw that she was travelling from Prijedor to Orlovci, and she told me that she lived in Orlovci. I knew her very well, but I did not know that she was actually living in Orlovci. So that is how we became closer. She very often needed us, not only she, there were residents of Orlovac who had to travel to Prijedor. There was a woman there who had to travel almost every day to the market. She took her dairy products to the market. There was a nurse living in Donji Orlovci and who was also travelling every day to Prijedor. So we met each other every day at the Orlovci checkpoint. It was when she was either going to work or coming back from work. We would often -- we had to stop their vehicles because we had to stop every single vehicle passing through the Orlovci checkpoint. So we always stopped them. Sometimes there would be 20 vehicles in a column because we had to check them. When it comes to military vehicles, there was military police who were working next to us and they had the same type of duty with the military vehicles. So, I knew the residents very well. Sometimes they would bring us coffee to the checkpoint. They were grateful to us because the only means of transport was actually hitchhiking or bicycles. But at that time there was no buses, and all vehicles available were being used for transport of soldiers to Gradacac or elsewhere and those vehicles were quite damaged because of the transport of military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: She told us that on occasions you would often stop a vehicle and arrange that the driver who had been stopped would have to take her as a passenger. Did you do that for her as well as other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was common for all people who lived there, not only for those who lived there, but there were people, for example, travelling to Banja Luka who had arrived to Orlovci from Prijedor and they were waiting for transport to Banja Luka, and that is how it worked. It was a very busy road for private transport, private cars, and for transport of goods because it was the main communication between the Krajina, the Knin Krajina, and Serbia. So it was a quite busy road. So, Slavica, yes, I saw her almost every day. I think that was the person whom I saw most frequently in Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time, as you have told us, you were living in Prijedor. How did you used to travel to your duty point at Orlovci from the centre of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have to leave half an hour before the beginning of my shift. So I would go to the police station in the centre of the Prijedor town. We would report there for duty. The shift changed in front of the building of the Prijedor police. Brdar was in charge of some kind of procedure for the changing of shifts. So I did not meddle into that, but I know that he was receiving some orders, whether from the Commander or his deputy, but anyhow he always had some kind of instructions as to what we should do, how we should behave. There was this vehicle, police vehicle, which would take all three of us there. Brdar was shift Commander, and that is how we went to work. That was the regular procedure and nothing unusual happened. It was quite organised. We had patrol orders, warrants. So each time we finished our shift, the number of kilometres would be entered in that book. So we were not allowed to drive more kilometres than normally necessary. He would have been responsible for that. He was responsible for the vehicle, fuels and so on. We had to be very careful with fuel at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said it was a police vehicle; was that a civilian vehicle used by the police or was it marked as a police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a police vehicle. It was a blue Golf with a radio station built in. That is how we maintain communication. That was the main means of transportation. In principle, we could not use the vehicle if there was some incident in Orlovci without clearing it with the centre; we could not do anything. So Brdar kept communications through this radio station and that is where he got instructions for his work. The vehicle was always parked at the very checkpoint facing the side of the road towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Travelling in the vehicle from the SUP in Prijedor to take you to the checkpoint, what would then happen to the vehicle once you had arrived at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vehicle was parked, the door open and a window wound down so that we could hear any communication via the radio station so that we could keep the communication open. Then we would go about doing the job that we were in charge of from before. We knew what our duties were. It was the control of civilian, both passenger and freight, traffic around Karlovac. So, our duties were exclusively with the civilian control. We had -- we were not authorised to control military vehicles or people in vehicles who had been mobilized to the military. Sometimes we would stop a civilian vehicle, and if the driver would show a military booklet, we could not control him. We were not allowed to. Then we would call over the military police and then they would do the control of those vehicles and those passengers. We were working exclusively the control, the transportation of goods and passengers in the civilian sector. The military police, it is true, had higher authorities. They could control both the civilian and the military traffic on that road, Orlovci/Prijedor. We had no right to control the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The military unit that you have referred to at Orlovci, was that at the same number of officers as you? Was that three soldiers or was it a different number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, mostly it was two soldiers, two military policemen. They wore military police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did the police car remain at Orlovci with you whilst you were on duty at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have a vehicle. Their shifts were different than ours. I do not remember exactly where their shifts were changed but, for the most part, they were transported by some vehicles. I think they had trucks, maybe a Pitzgauer. I do not know where they had their duties, but they had strange shifts and they had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am actually talking about the police car, did that remain at Orlovci with you whilst you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The translation, it was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hence the different answer, but I will repeat the question again. Did the police car remain at Orlovci with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of your shift did you return in the police car back to the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the vehicle -- after our duties, we would go back to in front of the police station and the shift was changing in front of the police station. We would show up early. We would leave -- that means the shift that was to take over, they would arrive early in front of the police station. So it could not happen that we would arrive there and not be met by somebody. The shift would then be done very fast. In the meantime, the military police would be on duty because they had authority to control both the civilian and military traffic. So, our absence was not really felt very much during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you go back in the police car to the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was always done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any right or was it part of your duties that you could leave Orlovci during your shift and travel somewhere else in the police car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not a chance of that taking place. This is what we were told right away by the Commander and then Brdar also, the chief of the shift, so that we could not do anything like that. Brdar was a very serious man perhaps because his wife's father had been a traffic policeman for 30 years, and maybe through living with them he gained knowledge about how things were happening. So, I do not know, but things were not happening that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived for your shift half an hour early to the police station to report. At the end of the shift how long did it take before you were officially at the end of your duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of your shift, when you had returned to the police station, was there a period of time that you had to wait at the police station as part of a handover before you were officially discharged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brdar would do the change of duty. When we were -- when we would come back in the vehicle in front of the police station, the police, the next shift would go immediately off to their duty. Brdar would always stay and do the paperwork. I know that he filed reports and that he communicated in that respect with the police. It was not my duty to stay around. Sometimes we worked 12 hours, sometimes all night. I was just looking to go back home as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were off duty from the police station, were you able to go free wherever you liked? Were you able to spend your free time away from the police out of the area travelling around or going wherever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not travel that easily. Every movement -- for every move, you had to report to the authorities. If you had something sudden, you had to call up, you had to report to the policeman on duty and tell them where you would be because our duty was to be present at the address where we lived. So that in case of unexpected, anything unexpected, we would be there at a moment's notice. I am not saying you could not leave, but you had to ask the authorities. If you wanted, for instance, to go somewhere the next day, you always had to get some kind of a certificate, some kind of a paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps at this stage if we could look at Exhibit 332A and B? If 332 in the English form can be put on the overhead monitor and the defendant have the version in Serbo-Croat? You have there, Mr. Tadic, a version in Serbo-Croat which we can see is a document signed by Simo Drljaca. It is a document issued by Prijedor SUP and saying that Dusko Tadic is authorised to travel between Prijedor, Kozarac and back, Palanciste, for the purpose of transporting firewood and items from the house. It is a document that is dated but it is unclear, according to the translation, when in June 1992 this date refers to. Are you able to help us with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I now remember, regardless of what it says here. It was on the first day when I came to Prijedor. Since I had proved that I lived in Kozarac, Marsala Tita Street, No. 36, I requested from the Chief of Police, I asked for a document so that I can go and evacuate certain items from my house. That was on the first day upon my arrival in Prijedor on the Monday, the day before I started my duty. That was the practice then. This is what you needed to get if you were to leave Prijedor on any basis. They always said, why, the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the date you are referring to would be 15th June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this certificate to be used on that date or could it be used on another date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This certificate was used on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you go to Kozarac on that date of 15th June from Prijedor to collect firewood and items from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What would have been the purpose of going on that particular date, the day before your official first duty date, to Kozarac to collect items from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
