utterances.text: The purpose was that I knew that I would be busy later, so I wanted to use the opportunity. I evacuated, kept evacuating things from my house throughout that year. I did not have an opportunity to have special vehicles. As I said, my brother paid for that one and even on that day I asked the man, I never paid him, and on this occasion I evacuated, removed, some of my belongings to Palanciste with my aunt Sava Vokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We heard evidence earlier in the trial from Sava Vokic. Did she live in that district of Palanciste?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She lives in Velika Palanciste in a large house by herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What goods did you collect from the Tadic family home then on that date when you went to her house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where it says that the permission is for items from the house, plus firewood, but again I did not know what I would find there. I learned from my previous experience that I did not know what was going to be there. On that day, I took some garden chairs from my cafe, so that is what we were using in the summer. Then some clothing because, in principle, it was very difficult to move the clothing. So there were some children's clothing and then I made bundles with white sheets. So that was, basically, what I took. It was not that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How were the goods transported on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whose truck did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Savanovic Slobodan's who used to live in Kozarac earlier, but I do not know at what period he moved to Prijedor with his wife, and I did not engage him specially. I just ran into him and I told him that I was going to Kozarac and he said, "Oh, yes, that would work for me too". I did not know that he was a professional trucker, but I used the opportunity to put some of my belongings there. I could not afford a special delivery. So when he was loading things from where he was working before the war, I also added some of my own. He worked in a building across where the same apartment block where Trivo Reljic worked, and his wife worked in a pharmacy in Kozarac, so they worked above it in the Marsala Tita Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this period that you were working at checkpoint Orlovci, was there another occasion when you went back to Kozarac to collect items or goods from the family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the beginning of July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that occasion did you have a certificate such as the one we see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but that time I actually engaged this man because I met him while working at the Orlovci checkpoint, Brane Koncar. I think he was a private trucker and he was from the village of Kalanj near Orlovci. I asked him, and we went to Kozarac together. We moved some goods to my relative Jankovic, very near Orlovci. I do not know what the name of the village is, I think Vlacine or something, maybe one kilometre from where we held the post at Orlovci. Jankovic, Dragoje, he is my distant relative. Our mothers are sisters. So he accepted to take some stuff. It was mostly some building supplies that in '92 I was preparing to finish the top part of my business premises, and it was an amount of construction supplies with which I was going to finish the attic part. Then I also brought the freezer unit and the stove, a wood stove, and I remember at that time I also brought a terrier dog. Then he kept it throughout that time. Then I do not know what happened. That was the mother of those two terrier puppies, the hunting dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that the Dragoje Jankovic we heard evidence from a few weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you left those goods at his place, how long did they remain there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those goods stayed there all the way up to '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The goods that you took to Palanciste, to Sava Vokic's home, how long did those goods remain there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Not all things stayed there till '93. I took the freezer and wood stove earlier, but the building supplies -- I do not know what the exact translation of that word is -- but that was -- that remained there. I needed it in Kozarac, so that remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned a man called Brane Koncar who helped you on the other visit in July. Do you know how many people called Brane Koncar there are in that region of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there are several. I do not know exactly. I know one Brane Koncar who used to live in Kozarac, but it is not the one. The one from Kozarac is very tall. He is about 1.9 metres tall, but Brane Koncar that I referred to, he is from the Kalate village and he is roughly my age ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know another ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- and I think he is blondish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- Brane Koncar who worked at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to these trips for which a certificate was issued, you have got this one still amongst your possessions. Was there any reason for keeping that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a reason, yes. First of all, we had a practice to keep all the documents of this kind to track the origin of these goods, because there were some machinations, that is, people were looting in Kozarac. It was very desirable to have a document stating the origin of your property. I know that I bought these building materials towards the end of '91. I had those documents too. I know when I was preparing it and many of my neighbours knew about it. They knew why I was preparing this. This is why I have kept this material. There were different kinds of controls. During 1992 certain commissions were established which went around to the centre of Prijedor or municipality and later we also did it, I did it later. We would inventory all the property that was undocumented. When we would -- the owner, if we found some materials and some property, we would ask for an explanation, where it came from. Then we made the reports and if they could not document it, it could be taken away from them. This is why I kept this documentation. I kept those materials all the way up until '93. That was one reason. The second, if you wanted to sell some of them, you again had to prove the origin of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what stage did your duties finish at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working at Orlovci in the early August and I moved to the Most Na Sani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have seen the checkpoint Orlovci official duty plan which contains your duty for 3rd August as being on the River Sana, on the bridge. Did you work there for only one shift or more than one shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only worked at that time and that was again with Cvijic. Brdar was not with us, only Miroslav Cvijic. After that, I think that it was on 6th we stopped working at the police, and Cvijic and I went to talk with the Commander, and then we were transferred to work with the police, the general police. So we continued to work, but we were secured -- part of security detailed for the Security Centre building, and we continued to work there another few days, maybe, until 10th or 11th August '92 and Cvijic remained on that duty for some time longer and I was transferred to secure the railway and bus station in Prijedor, where I worked until the end of August 1992 and the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at that period as a whole from the beginning of June until the beginning of August 1992. During that time did you ever visit the camp at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During that time did you ever visit the camp at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have referred to the single visit with Jovo Samardzija at the beginning of June 1992. During that period of time did you ever visit the camp at Trnopolje again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean between June and August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: June and the middle of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The flat that you told us about in Prijedor in Pecani that you moved into on 27th June 1992, did you continue to reside in that flat for the rest of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of 1992 I continued to live in Pecani, B2, third floor. I have to say that in all my life I have not been to the Ljubija ore mine before, during or after the war in the Prijedor municipality area. I never set foot in there. I was never there officially, privately. I was not forced to go there. I had no business there. So I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In August 1992, did you apply to open a cafe bar in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is actually a convenient moment before I enter into a completely new subject.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you worked after you had been with the reserve traffic police for other stations within Prijedor police station, and you gave those details. When did you start working for the Kozarac police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started working for the Kozarac police as of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did the transfer from the Prijedor police to the Kozarac police occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a matter of procedure relating to our activities on the revival of Kozarac. It was not only transformation of the police station in Kozarac, the transformation of the police station in Prijedor into police station in Kozarac, but it was a process related to the establishment of the Local Commune in Kozarac. It did not happen all at once. There were quite a few difficulties in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you start to become involved then with the return to Kozarac and the revival of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, activities in relation to the return to Kozarac were launched by a certain number of residents of Kozarac who at that time were living in Prijedor as refugees, displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what happened at the beginning, at first, we did not know what kind of perspective my native town had, the town where I wanted to return very soon, but at the beginning of August 1992 an information was made public that the municipal Crisis Staff has reached a decision that Kozarac would not be resettled and that no one would return there. So, in view of those circumstances, I met with many people from Kozarac there. I first met with Bosko Dragicevic and then I also met with Ivo Rajkovic and many others who were living in Kozarac. I also met some neighbours of mine of Muslim nationality. I used to run into them throughout that summer, and I talked to them, we exchanged opinions, we consulted with each other, and I also talked to Meho Beslagic about that. I talked to former President of the Court in Prijedor, Tadzic Hamzalija, and we were just discussing the activities that would be adequate at that time. So we said that nothing would happen if we do not undertake something. So, while in Orlovci, I several times met the Commander of the regional Crisis Staff, Vinko Kos, who was very cynical and whenever he passed the Orlovci checkpoint he would ask me, "Where is your Kozarac? Kozarac has come to nothing now. We are the power. We will be deciding about your fate", and so on. So, when this public information was given that Kozarac would not be resettled, we became active, several, five or six of us, me, Bosko Dragicevic, Goran Babic, Ivo Rajkovic, and many others. Many Muslims were also involved in that, but they avoided direct contact with the Prijedor municipalities. Because of their former experience, they did not want to meet those people who were then in power in Prijedor. But everybody was informed of that, and we were trying to undertake something so that that should be -- that could be avoided. Lamovita was just a village which consisted of 20 houses and did not have a sewer system, nothing. It was absurd, the situation, where that village was becoming more important than Kozarac which had several thousands of houses, several thousands of telephone numbers. The elementary school in Kozarac was one of the biggest elementary schools in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kozarac itself is over 200 years older than Prijedor. So we were all emotionally involved in that and we simply could not allow it to happen. So, there was an initiative which was launched by us, Bosko Dragicevic and several other people. We know that other villages such as Balte, Vidovici and Podgradje, that there were some Serbian residents still living there and that those people were actually the only residents of the Kozarac Local Commune. So we had a meeting with the President of the Executive Council of the Prijedor municipality, Mico Kovacevic, and he said, "Well, it is a decision of the Executive Committee. There is nothing to be changed". But then we wanted to contact the then President of the SDS, and he told us that there was a procedure, except that the problem was that at that time in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor Kozarac did not have its representatives in Prijedor. So people from Kozarac could by no means influence decisions which were being reached for them. The absolute power from the beginning of the conflict until the end of 1992 was in the hands of Crisis Committees, the municipal Crisis Committee and the regional Crisis Committee. So, I learned that the municipality had been divided into regional Crisis Staff who had its Commanders and its delegates to the municipal Crisis Committee who was in charge of everything, all kind of decisions. They had an absolute power at that moment, both civilian and military. We talked to Simo Miskovic and at that time in the summer of 1992 they were not active at all. The political parties were not working, not only the SDS, but other parties as well, the Party of Reforms and so on. So we became active and we went to the village of Balte. I remember that we first went to Kozarac. I did that in addition to my duties in August, so whenever I was free I had talks and then we would go together to Kozarac. I remember we contacted Mirko Grahovac several times who had a tractor so we would visit those villages in his tractor. We discussed the situation, and we knew that such was the procedure after the Second World War. So we were driving along macadams. We did not -- nobody had a car and even if we had had a car there was no fuel. So the situation was very problematic. So, we went to those villages and we informed people about that decision, and we told them that Kozarac would simply disappear if nothing was done. People were, of course, against that because they knew Kozarac, although it had been destroyed, had infrastructure, very valuable infrastructure, telephones and everything that was necessary for an urban area. So, we met in Prijedor and I remember we were received by the then Vice President of the Executive Council of the municipality and who was also a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, Bosko Mandic, whom I have known before as a sportsman. He knew me as well, but when we met there were over 50 of us present at that meeting and he was surprised. He said, "I did not know that you were 50 in Kozarac, people both of Muslim and Croatian nationality. I thought that you were only two or three". That is how that meeting was held. Some people of Croatian nationality attended those meetings as well, and they asked whether they could go back and live in Kozarac. They addressed the question to that person. There were no people of Muslim nationality, but they were also active and they wanted something to be undertaken in that respect, especially the former President of the Court in Prijedor, and then a neighbour of mine, Beslagic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are going very fast again, Mr. Tadic, and all this information has to be absorbed and translated. So if you could go more slowly, all right? What was the date then that this idea that Kozarac had a chance of being revived came about? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we -- at that time we were not aware, we did not know, whether the municipal Crisis Staff would alter their decision. Miskovic told us that there was a procedure through which we could alter that, but we needed a forum of citizens who were interested in that, so we needed a formal application. We did not know much about that because I talked, for example, to Vinko Kos and he was telling me that there was simply no way. They even had some agreements that Kozarac should be completely destroyed, levelled, and I personally became aware of that and I would not have reacted that fast had I not seen that machines were in Kozarac and that the destruction of Kozarac had already began. I remember seeing at the beginning of August on the right side of the road between Koncari and Kozarac and also on the main road Prijedor/Banja Luka, at the beginning of August, some 20 houses had been already completely destroyed. There was nothing there. The area had been cleared out by the earth moving equipment. So he told me that the same was awaiting the left side of the road and that they were planning to have some military barracks there. I asked him, "Why?" I failed to see any reason for that. I simply could not understand that people who had taken over power in Prijedor, I mean, the regional Crisis Staff in Lamovita, I could not understand their intentions, but such were their intentions and they proposed that because Zivko Kos was a member of the regional Crisis Staff in Lamovita, and he was a member of the SDS in Kozarac, in the Local Commune of Kozarac. He was the only person from the area, from the former Local Commune in Kozarac, and at that time there were no deputies in the municipality. So those people were supposed to represent the interests of the Kozarac Local Commune. I was surprised to hear that. So we took an initiative of our own, some 20 of us from the centre of Kozarac, and we had the first meeting between 10th and 13th August in the building of the Municipal Assembly, Prijedor. We made an official request to have the decision altered, the decision which had been reached by the Executive Council of Prijedor. Bosko Mandic told us that he would inform the local board of our request and the President was Mico Kovacevic, and that we would receive an answer within several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have seen a document dated 15th August 1992 which set out a constitution for the SDS party in Kozarac. How did that come about that the SDS party at that time was establishing itself within the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would ask, if possible, to have a look at that document. I can explain, but it would be much easier because it was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- an usual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 333, please. There is an (A) and (B), I think. If the English can be put on the overhead monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is of the same date and if we could have Exhibit 149?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because that document has more details about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps then that 333 can be taken off the monitor and just put on one side down here and if you can 149 and the English version of 149 put on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that these documents can be understood only if they are looked at as a whole, because it is difficult -- it does not mean much, one without the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document, the one we are now looking at, Exhibit 149, has a number of names written upon it. It records that the decision taken at an Assembly of the SDS on the date of 15th August was that you would be President of the Kozarac local board of the SDS. How did it come about that you were to be President as a result of the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about the following. Based on an initiative of a member of the Executive Council, Bosko Mandic, he explained to us what the procedure was if we wanted to re-establish, if we wanted to start again, the Local Commune. We could not undertake anything before the decision of the Executive Council in Prijedor is altered, because that decision said clearly that the Local Commune in Kozarac did not exist. So, several days later we went there again, Bosko Dragicevic, myself and several other people, and they showed us a document by which the former decision was revoked. So, it was written on that document that they were agreeable as to re-establishment of the Local Commune in Kozarac. At that time nothing functioned in Kozarac. There was no Local Commune and Local Commune did not have its regular bodies. There was no Executive Board of the Local Commune. There was not any political party which could represent people in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you form a local board of the SDS in Kozarac as a way of attempting to influence the decision that had been taken in Prijedor by the party in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Without an organised approach, it was not possible to alter the decision. They gave us their approval as to the initiative on the work of the Local Commune in Kozarac. However, we knew that the representatives of the SDA from Kozarac were no longer active in Prijedor, and the SDA in Prijedor was in existence, but the same went for other political parties. Two people who were active before were Zivko Kos and Vinko Kos, but they had no interest in that whatsoever. They were a member of the Crisis Staff at that time and they even expressed their disapproval as to the work of the Local Commune in Kozarac. So, in order to have anything done, we had to have a Citizens Assembly in the Local Commune of Kozarac, regardless of their number. So that is how we convened Citizens Assembly and it was held on 15th August 1992. It was attended by the then Vice President of the municipality, Dragan Savanovic, because we wanted to give it some sort of legitimacy. Here it says, "Chairman, Goran Borovnica". He was instituted formally because he had certain merits from the war, and there was a proposal of a certain number of people because we did not have any experience in the war and we did not have anything to be proud of. So, Goran Borovnica accepted to be Chairman, but only for that Assembly. He was acting as Chairman until the President of the Local Commune in Kozarac was elected. At the beginning of the meeting, the President of the Assembly was elected. It was Bosko Dragicevic. Such was the procedure. After the President of the Assembly was elected, he put up an agenda and on the agenda was the initiative to create, to establish a local board of the SDS in Kozarac. On the same day, in order for everything to be legitimate, the Assembly of the Local Commune elected the local board. At that time there were not enough members of the SDS from the area of Kozarac, and that is why here you have a number of 15, but we did not have anyone else. So we proposed 14 people, because we simply could not find the 15th one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you appointed as President of the local board of the SDS for Kozarac by authorities outside Kozarac, say, Prijedor or elsewhere, or were you the choice of those who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you what the procedure was. Vice President of the municipality, Dragan Savanovic, was there and he was watching the meeting, and then a certain number of people proposed for the President of the Assembly -- and that Bosko Dragicevic was elected. After that, they voted for the President of the local board of the SDS and its members, members of the local board. That is why I was not appointed. I was chosen. Here you have decision on elections for the Kozarac local board of the SDS, not a decision on the appointment, but election. It is true that there are many things in this paper, but you should look at them separately, but everything was done step by step, but in one day. That is why here you have decision, elections and then appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You sometimes have an appointment after an election, you see, which is why I asked the questions I did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at Exhibit 333. Here we see a document that is headed: "A decision on the constitution of the Kozarac branch of the SDS". On this date of 15th August 1992 the acting President is cited as being Goran Borovnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it all happened on the same day. That is why I told you that you should look at these documents in parallel. There may be something unclear here, because everything took place on the same day, at the same meeting, at the same session. They elected the President of the Assembly of the Local Commune, and the Assembly of the Local Commune then proposed establishment. It was a constitutional Assembly at the same time. They suggested that the local board of the SDS should be established. This might be somewhat unusual, but there was not any other way because in Kozarac at that time there were not enough members of the SDS. So, if 200 people from the SDS had been present, it would be different, but at that time you only had about 14 people. So this is a legitimate decision. I remember it very well. It might be unusual, but the Assembly of the Local Commune, that is, the totality of the population living there, they established the Local Commune of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have covered this already. So I want to turn now to the Kozarac Commune where you were appointed Secretary of the Commune. If we can look at document Exhibit 334?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but I wish to add something in relation to paragraphs 2, 3, 5 and 6 -- 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe we will come back to that. I do not want to get bogged down too much in the detail of that as I do not see it as being important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I have to tell you that in paragraph No. 3 which states that the local board of the SDS at that time was verified by the Citizens Assembly, that it had taken over the responsibilities and duties of the Council of the Local Commune of Kozarac, but at that time there was no Council. So the local board of the SDS by a decision of the Assembly of the Local Community took over responsibility of the Council of the local board which was established in October 1992. That is all I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go to Exhibit 334. If the English can be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the witness. This is a document where we see that the Chairman of the Citizens Assembly that you told us about, Bosko Dragicevic, signed it. It concerns a meeting of 22nd August 1992. It is a decision on the resumption of work of the Kozarac Local Commune. Is it right again that this was part of the procedure that was attempting to start work to revive Kozarac after the impact of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This document and these decisions here were preceded by some meetings, meetings that were held on 15th August 1992, without what meetings it would have been impossible to reach any kind of decision whatsoever. On the basis of this decision the municipal Crisis Staff in Prijedor could react. They were sent one copy and they were thus forced to revoke the decision, the first decision in relation to the Local Commune in Kozarac, because this decision was based on previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did they revoke that decision in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision was revoked after we sent this decision, our decision. We had had talks previously in the Prijedor town hall, but after we established the local board of the SDS and after we elected the President of the Council and the President of the Local Commune Assembly, we had a basis, a grounds for our request. Here, and this is the most important of our decisions, it says, "After the war operations in the territory of Kozarac the Kozarac Local Commune resumed its work." That was the result of everything that had happened before. They simply could not do anything against this particular decision. They simply had to alter their previous decision, and by "they" I mean members of the municipal Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look now at Exhibit 335 dated 31st August 1992, if the English could be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the defendant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot to tell you, you have here the signature of Bosko Dragicevic. You have to ask yourselves why there is no mention of Goran Borovnica here. He was only Chairman at one session until the President of the Local Commune was elected, that was Bosko Dragicevic and he worked as the President of the Assembly until the end of '92. In '93 that was the highest political function within the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think you have made that clear to us, that at the initial meeting someone who was a local figure, and you told us about him being involved in the war, had to take the chair for the meeting and then appointments were made as a result of the elections afterwards. Looking at document 335, we can see here that this is a programme for the local board of the SDS in relation to events within the Local Commune. Again, this date of 31st August 1992, was it important because decisions were able thereafter to be made relating to improvement of the condition of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this decision was part of decisions, previous decisions which began as of 15th August. It was not maybe done very professionally, because we were never really politically active in relation to the work of the Local Commune. So, this may not be very professional, but we did have a written basis for activities that followed in the Local Commune in Kozarac. On 31st August 1992 not all bodies of the Local Commune in Kozarac functioned. There was a period which preceded the real work of the Local Commune in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 151, and again if the English could be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the defendant. This is a document dated 9th November 1992, but it refers to the decision on 31st August and refers to the election of the Kozarac Local Commune Secretary on 9th November. Can you tell us about this document which refers to the earlier dates, and in paragraph two refers to the competition of 9th September 1992: "Dusko Tadic from Kozarac has been appointed Kozarac Local Commune Secretary"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This decision refers to the decision of 31st August 1992, and relates mainly to the work of the Local Commune. It is impossible for a local commune to function without a secretary of the Local Commune, a fully employed secretary of the Local Commune. A secretary was always a professional position, but it had nothing to do with the party activity, the work of the political parties. I do not know whether you have a decision on the competition. The decision on the appointment was preceded by competition for the position of the secretary to the Local Commune. That competition is mentioned here in paragraph two. So on the basis of the competition of 9th September 1992, Dusko Tadic from Kozarac has been appointed for the Local Commune Secretary. So there had been competition before. Anybody could apply for that position, but I remember that period very well. That competition was open and it was publicly announced in Prijedor on the books, such was the procedure. So it was publicly announced, but nobody applied for it simply because people had no interest whatsoever to go and work in Kozarac in view of its state. I remember I was the only one who showed any interest in taking up that position. So the decision on the appointment of the Kozarac Local Commune Secretary was reached by the Assembly of the Kozarac Local Commune, the very same Assembly. I mean all the citizens, all the residents, of the Kozarac Local Commune. Here you have mention of the President of the Assembly of the Local Commune which was always the highest body in the Local Commune. At that time the President was Bosko Dragicevic, and he was the Chairman at that meeting when I was elected Secretary to the Local Commune. All these decisions relate to the beginning of the work of the Kozarac Local Commune. It was the period of August 1992, and during that period there were not many people who were interested in doing anything in Kozarac. In respect to June 1992 the time of my first visit, it was already -- it had changed. It was something like we have seen here on video. It was not the same place, the same place I visited the first time I went there. It was systematically destroyed, although it was in the jurisdiction of the municipal Crisis Staff. There were some people who were providing security, but there were also many military formations in Kozarac at that time who were ostensibly protecting the town, but ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time were you also involved with the Kozarac local police as well as starting this project of working in Kozarac trying to restore the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from early September 1992, maybe that is why it is unclear in the documents, but it is a procedure when at the beginning of September I became part of the revival of Kozarac and I still had duties with securing the railway and bus station in Prijedor. So that I was often and for the most part in the field all day. So, if I was on duty at the bus station in Prijedor, at say 9.00 o'clock in the evening, so the whole morning I would spend in Kozarac with these assistants and then I would come to duty and then after a while I just could not take it any more. That whole activity started in August and then finally physically I was just not able to do it any more. So that was the reason why I moved from the police, from the Prijedor police to the Kozarac police, because it was not possible to leave the police. Had I left then I would have been mobilized, I would be would have been conscripted. It would not have been possible to interrupt the duties as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you cease working for the Kozarac local police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working exactly on 19th November 1992. However, the same month though, I think it was on 6th November, I got days off from the Commander of the police station because I was involved in different committees, different commissions, which worked on the revival. It was about markings which is what we saw. There were circles with crosses. The first action that we had was the protection of the structures that were in the centre of Kozarac. The only way to do it legally was to form a municipal commission that was to find out the conditions of the residential fund in Kozarac. Blue, red and white signified the -- and the difference in colours as you may have been able to see -- each colour signified a certain degree of destruction. This work was done by the Municipal Commission from Prijedor, and it was the precondition for any kind of reconstruction of these structures. So that was taking a picture of the conditions of the residential buildings, and this was the first time -- the centre of Kozarac was not destroyed. Maybe there were damages, maybe 20 per cent, but 80 per cent of the damage that ensued happened later in the period between June 1992 and the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time which really begins from the middle of August 1992 when you are attempting to restore Kozarac and onwards, did you have refugees coming into the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was another reason why we raised our voice against those activities, simply because we were surprised when we saw from the beginning of July 1992, I worked at the checkpoint Orlovci, I saw the refugees coming through. It was true that they had been expelled from their own homes where they used to live before, but it is also true that they could have moved into the centre of Kozarac. I still claim that had those people moved there Kozarac would not have been destroyed. It is true that people who never lived there would have now been living there, but it would not have been destroyed. So the regional Crisis Staff of Trnopolje organised this activity and they moved some people in that area of Trnopolje. As I said, before the regional Crisis Staff had been formed and the one in Trnopolje was covered and overnight they brought a decision that their area comprised from the railroad tracks to the main road to Kozarac, and the centre of Kozarac, which was the most valuable, was now belonging to the regional Crisis Staff in Lamovita who decided that it was not going to be revived. So they never wanted to protect it and they never had any intentions of protecting it. So if you look at Hrnici, Suhi Brod and the other parts there, that is where people live. That is where in July and August people were moved in, organised by the regional Crisis Staff of Trnopolje thinking that it was incumbent upon them to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you were Secretary of the Local Commune, did that count as a form of work obligation that meant that you did not have to be mobilized for the military and undertake military duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reason which followed out of all these activities. It would not have been possible to work as a Secretary of the Local Commune and continue working in the police. But from the takeover of power in Prijedor and on, I was getting more and more an impression that there was a split, a schism. The SDS had no activity. They stopped their activity and the Crisis Staff took over all activities. Because of the events, the dominant positions were occupied by the military personnel, by officers, and the war zones and the war effort was given the highest priority. Everything else was neglected. As far as the work duties are concerned, I have to say one more thing. One of the reasons maybe why I was not mobilized before June 16th 1992 -- there are several reasons. One of the reasons is that I acted the way I did, in other words I was in Banja Luka. The other one is that 10 years before the I mostly was in private business and at one time even in Banja Luka, and at that time I was tied militarily to my firm, to my company and while I was in Croatia. That is why I was never mobilized for the war in Croatia, in the first place. Also in the former Yugoslavia people who were in private business were almost never mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At one stage you were issued with a certificate which excused you from the military as a result of your position as Secretary of the Local Commune which counted as your work obligation, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That request by the procedure was produced by the Executive Board of the Local Commune in Kozarac, but it had not been acted on. It was not acted on until early 1993. Simply, I was still from 19th November on, I was free of that, but there was always a possibility to be involved in any police activity in Kozarac. But because of this procedure until the end of, up towards the end of 1992 I was already freed of these obligations, so I worked as Secretary for the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at Prosecution Exhibit 154. We see here a document that is -- if the English can be put on the overhead monitor -- the decision on the assignment of work obligations. This document states that your post as Secretary of the Local Commune in Kozarac is to be considered a combat assignment, and if there is a call for mobilization you should report immediately to the post you were assigned to. Were there in fact attempts by the military to mobilize you and put you within the military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Although you had an exemption by reason of your work obligation, were the military in fact accepting that as being something that you were able to use to avoid being mobilized within the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beside this one, on 25th December 1992 I was permanently removed from the list of the reserve police force, and that was always a problem. The cessation of duties towards a unit of any kind was always when you got the final seal in the military booklet. So my first entry, the first seal is on 16th June, and the last day I think is 25th December 1992. My obligation ceased both regarding the military and the police. At that time I was officially fully employed as Secretary for the Local Commune. The procedure that the Assembly made in order for me not to be recalled to the military or the police, was completed with this decision when I was put in the position of Secretary of the Local Commune. Here it says, "conscript". Any person, regardless of whether they were police or the military, had a military obligation. So that where it later says that one should report to a post, according to this decision it says, it is a post to where I should report in the future and that meant from this date on. It meant the position of the Secretary of the Local Commune. So this is my post. That was also my workplace as of that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there attempts by the military to forcibly enlist you for military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did those attempts by the military take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those activities started first in March 1993 and up to August 1993. In other words, half a year I was exposed to the military police in Prijedor. In the first period, from March till June 1992 I was arrested several times by the military police. I would always show them this document. The patrol leaders at that time told me that this is a document which obligated them to release me. So they could not mobilize me without revoking this decision, and this decision could only be revoked by the men in charge of the National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The witness has said March till June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. [To the witness]: Was that right, March till June 1992 you were arrested several times by the police? Is that the right year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if we just slow things down a little bit, Mr. Tadic, which is why I am searching for a document. It is always a useful recourse. Can we have Exhibit D8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can, I started reading this ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. If you can just wait for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was translated this is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us just go to a document here which will tie matters in. If page 15 of the English can be put on the monitor and if you could put this in front of the witness. I would like you to look at section 10. Section 10 of the military book shows your participation in war and it has your mobilization date of 16th June 1992. That date you told us of, 25th December 1992. Did that not release you then from any further obligation, taking into account that decision that you had on the assignment of your work obligations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the decision made on the work obligation was made in early '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Why then in 1993 were the military forces attempting to mobilize you contrary to your exemption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was absolutely illegal, and it was illegal relative to the laws of Republika Srspka. They could not have mobilized me. It was illegal of them. As far as the stamps are concerned, the first stamp is the security services centre, that is an old stamp of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I know its shape, and the last stamp is the stamp of Republika Srpska, also the police stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We also see as part of this section 10 the date of 10th June 1993. Was that a date that you were mobilized at the front by the military?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may have to move it. Is it on this Exhibit, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. If you can move it up the screen a bit. I am sorry, your Honour. Thank you. Section two as translated. Is that the date that you were mobilized at the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the stamp of the military. As I said, it was illegal because on 10th June I had a work obligation as a Secretary of the Local Commune. The real procedure was to revoke that decision by the Ministry of Defence office in Prijedor, and only then could they make decisions about my assignment to the police or the military. So they had no right to do that. I remember that I visited Slavko Budimir on this matter and he said that he could not revoke this decision because I was fully employed as a Secretary of the Local Commune. I was being paid, given a salary, and the Assembly of both Kozarac and Prijedor had to be involved in the process. So he had no answer why they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Stop there. How many attempts had been made to arrest you before you were mobilized on 10th June 1993? Do not give me the details, just the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From March until this date, five or six attempts. Sometimes I jumped out of the window. Sometimes I would take cover from where I was sitting, but there were several attempts in Kozarac to arrest me. Several times the military police came. I would show them the documents. They would not arrest me, but they had an arrest warrant for me. They said, "It is all fine, we have other people, but for some reason they want to arrest you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On 10th June 1993 where were you mobilized to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that date I was arrested in Kozarac at the gas station, and a patrol chief, his name was Desimir, and his colleague, I think his name was Lajic, they took me to Prijedor in a van with another group of people. On the same day transferred me to the war zone near Gradacac. They told me in Kozarac they were taking me in for an information conversation, and I told them that I had a uniform and should I bring it. They said, "No. No, we are just taking you in for an interview" -- Vujicic was his name -- "and you will be released immediately." Their headquarters were in the fire station. I was surprised when I was just given travel documents. They said: "Take him to Gradacac." I said: "What interview in Gradacac?" They said: "Everything is fine. You are going to an interview with the Chief of the Military Security who is near Gradacac and you have to talk to him. He is there so you have to go there." They did not tell me that I would be put in a unit. They just told me there would be an interview, a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you taken then to the front at Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the front at Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They first took me to the command in Srednja Slatina. I waited for an hour and then that Desimir came out and said: "The Chief of Police is not going to talk to you. We have orders to put you in on the first line of fire." So they took me to that zone, into that zone, and that is where I spent the first night. Nobody gave me a weapon or told me anything, to sign up for anything. So they just brought me there and they left me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you remain serving at Gradacac or did you terminate your duty early?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day I escaped from there. I remember I saw Jozo Popovic there who was also mobilized as a civilian. So I was not the only one, but I did not want to leave it at that. So I met a truck driver who was bringing in food supplies and I asked him if he would help me get out of that there, and he said that he would. So I took a ride with him. I hid in the truck when it was returning. I did not know that area, otherwise I would have left on foot. That was not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you desert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not consider myself a deserter. I left because it was illegal. They considered it desertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until the following day).

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
(The Court adjourned for a short time)
